Across dense and weight-sparse checkpoints of the same transformer, evaluated on atomic and compositional proofs, we vary which extracted object is reported: a compact prediction-preserving circuit, a broader graph retaining surrounding read, write, and routing structure, or a subgraph extracted with a post-ablation loss budget. First, overlap between groups of component-to-component connections is low, sometimes close to a random baseline. Overlap is much higher for selected attention-head sets under deterministic selection, but falls sharply when selection among equally scored heads is randomized. Second, the normalized graph-size ranking of conditions that differ in which supervised checkpoint initializes reinforcement learning (RL) agrees between repeated extractions of the compact circuit and between joint and separate query/key representations of each of the other two graphs. For the loss-budgeted graph, query/key ordering agreement persists through the budget sweep. Finally, across those same conditions, the largest exact-match accuracy gains from RL on compositional proofs come with the largest proportion of components in the compositional

14c89fc74b2a5112a2ca0166.excerpt: arXiv:2607.21556v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes the external teacher required by on-policy distillation (OPD), but still needs asymmetric information between teacher and student so that the self-teacher provides a stronger learning signal. Existing methods create this asymmetry through privileged answers or visual evidence. We ask whether both can be removed, yielding a simpler form of OPSD driven purely by input conditioning. We propose Visual Contrastive Self-Distillation, namely VCSD, which converts image-content removal into an on-policy self-distillation signal. At each student-generated response prefix, the EMA teacher produces two next-token distributions under the same prompt and prefix: one conditioned on the original image and the other on a content-erased control. Their token-wise log-probability difference highlights candidates whose likelihood is specifically increased by the instance-level visual content. We use this contrast to sharpen the teacher's original-image distribution within its plausible support, and distill the resulting full-distribution target into the student. On ViRL39K, VCSD consistently outperforms matched OPSD across Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 models. It improves the seven-benchmark aggregate from 72.51% to 76.26% on Qwen3-VL-8B and from 74.97% to 79.24% on Qwen3.5-9B, with gains at all six evaluated scales. VCSD requires no external teacher, privileged answers, visual evidence signals, reasoning

b2fbeea2ff5e9ab86f530219.title_original: Filling Before Advancing: Capability-Gap-Driven Post-Training for Scenario-Specialized Remote Sensing MLLMs
b2fbeea2ff5e9ab86f530219.excerpt: arXiv:2607.22205v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Remote sensing multimodal large language models (RS-MLLMs) have advanced aerial-image understanding, but scenario specialization remains constrained by scarce high-quality supervision and incomplete capability coverage. We propose filling before advancing (FBA), a capability-gap-driven post-training route that develops prerequisite capabilities before scenario-specific adaptation. For coastal harbor understanding, we construct CPRS (Coastal-Port Remote Sensing), a three-layer dataset covering RGB, SAR, PAN, and NIR imagery. FBA organizes supervision into RS semantic anchoring, multi-source bridging, and evidence-grounded scenario tuning. We also introduce HarborEval, an eight-track benchmark assessing perception, spatial understanding, robustness, and generation. Using the same final-task supervision pool, FBA raises the HarborEval score from 57.95 to 70.29 on LLaVA-v1.5 and from 81.09 to 83.37 on Qwen3-VL compared with Direct-SFT. It also outperforms collapsed training and leads the evaluated comparisons on harbor-related VRSBench and RSVQA subsets and expert-scored OpenEval. Stage-wise and supervision-replacement analyses examine the contributions of the supervision roles. A lightweight urban instantiation further supports cross-scenario applicability, with the proposed stage order achieving stronger overall performance than the tested alternatives. Project resources and release updates are available at https://githu

c267e02e63a77ec59a77e426.title_original: Don't Regenerate, Debug: A Domain-Specific Agent for Repairing Near-Miss Accelerator Kernels
c267e02e63a77ec59a77e426.excerpt: arXiv:2608.02712v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Kernel generation for hardware accelerators such as GPUs and NPUs has become a proving ground for large language models (LLMs), and state-of-the-art systems raise correctness through pipelines that couple LLMs with agentic reinforcement learning and evolutionary search. Such pipelines generate, compile, and execute large numbers of candidate kernels, discarding most of them and forgoing the opportunity to distill failures into reusable knowledge. Many discarded candidates are near-miss operators that compile and run but fail numerical validation; each embodies genuine domain knowledge and a nontrivial investment in LLM inference, cross-compilation, and hardware execution. We argue for a paradigm shift: rather than regenerate, debug. Debugging is far more constrained than generating from scratch: the search space is small and feedback is dense. We present a domain-specific debug agent that addresses three core challenges in autonomous repair: mitigating knowledge scarcity through retrieved patterns and diagnostic instrumentation, ensuring integrity through anti-cheat detection and full-coverage evaluation, and controlling cost via convergence guards and bounded iteration. Debugging serves two complementary roles: it extends the capability frontier by recovering operators that repeated regeneration fails to produce, and it lowers cost per deliverable operator. Debug Pass@1 achieves 66.7% versus Regenerate Avg Pass@1's 25

d236da2e211d959fe779d66a.title_original: ValueFormer: Stage-Aware Value Labels for Online Failure Detection and VLA Post-Training
d236da2e211d959fe779d66a.excerpt: arXiv:2608.02958v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies now transfer to new scenes with little task-specific training, but they still fail silently: from the action stream alone, a collapsing rollout looks much like one making clean progress, because imitation supplies no notion of progress. The cheap alternative, a terminal success / failure bit, is learnable in principle yet too sparse to say when a rollout went wrong. We argue that the per-frame label is the hard part, and that it works better when continuous and non-monotonic: a score rather than a single success or failure, and one free to fall and then rise again as a rollout goes wrong and recovers. Such a label is cheap to obtain: a person marks only the stage at which an episode went wrong, and the per-frame values are computed from that. We present ValueFormer, a policy-agnostic causal transformer (3.5M parameters) over a frozen DINOv3 backbone, emitting two per-frame signals in one forward pass: a smooth Monte Carlo value for advantage estimation and a sharp binary value for online mistake detection. Failed episodes carry a stage-aware, success-then-decay return. A teleoperation station already records an intervention flag; reusing it lifts held-out detection from 0.38 to 0.82 average precision and flags 95% of mistakes before the operator reacts. On a real bimanual sandwich station, feeding the critic back as a per-frame post-training weight raises task completion

6a8b4903fcb99d789b593f66.title_original: MasDrift: Benchmarking Authorization Preservation Across Multi-Agent Architectures
6a8b4903fcb99d789b593f66.excerpt: arXiv:2608.07556v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) decompose long-horizon tasks across supervisors and subagents, but delegated goals do not necessarily carry their original authorization boundaries. Existing safety benchmarks mainly study adversarial compromise, while work on constraint drift lacks controlled architecture-level evaluation. We introduce MasDrift, a benchmark of 600 benign productivity tasks across eight domains. Each task pairs required work with reserved actions. MasDrift compares single-agent, centralized, and decentralized coordination while varying hierarchy depth and peer width, measuring task completion and authorization preservation. Across generic multi-agent conditions, centralized hierarchies achieve 93.9--98.6% task completion versus 85.7--87.0% for peer networks, while unauthorized actions occur in 2.7--19.8% of tasks versus 0.6--0.8%, a gap that widens with hierarchy depth. We further compare two defenses that differ in where authorization evidence resides. One re-anchors every pending call to the original user request. The other carries an attenuated policy along the delegation chain. Re-anchoring reduces unauthorized actions in every model configuration we evaluate, at a cost of 1.6 points of pooled completion. Chain propagation blocks required work instead, forfeiting up to 36.3 points. A heterogeneous case study confirms that the failure follows from coordination rather than model strength. MasDrift exposes a

c556cb4c5fe88aba7788bb33.title_original: DataKernelBench: Can LLMs Optimize Database Queries on GPUs?
c556cb4c5fe88aba7788bb33.excerpt: arXiv:2608.25061v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: GPUs increasingly accelerate database systems, but query-specific peak performance still often relies on hand-written kernels. Existing LLM kernel benchmarks focus on machine learning operators, leaving irregular, heterogeneous, data-movement-heavy database-style operators untested. We introduce DataKernelBench, which translates SQL into validated PyTorch TorchPlan programs and evaluates LLMs that optimize either the core tensor-bounded snippet or the full query in CUDA or Triton through execution-guided repair. Across ten proprietary and open-weight models on TPC-H SF10 with an H100 GPU, the strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieves $2.11\times$ speedup over the TorchPlan baseline at full pass rate. We find that higher-performing implementations commonly use kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes, stronger models benefit most from full-query specialization, and workload context matters more than hardware context. To handle data larger than GPU memory, we extend TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF for on-demand partition loading on TPC-H SF100 with four H100 GPUs, achieving $2.54\times$ speedup. Project page: https://kerneldf.github.io/datakernelbench

7740ab814dd27e86b1b6d15e.title_original: Spec-Driven Development as Prescribed and as Practiced
7740ab814dd27e86b1b6d15e.excerpt: arXiv:2608.25202v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI coding agents implement software from naturallanguage instructions, but the intent behind that work is lost when stated only in chat sessions. Spec-driven development (SDD) addresses this by having developers and agents write specifications that guide implementation, yet evidence on its use comes largely from tool vendors. We study SDD in practice through a thematic analysis of Reddit discussions, interviews with 21 practitioners, including eight tool makers, and 266 active and popular repositories in SpecMine, a corpus of 470,795 spec files from 73,030 public GitHub repositories that we release. Practitioners agreed that specs should capture intent, but many also included implementation details, used SDD selectively and mainly for new features, and reported more reliable agent behavior alongside greater planning and review costs. Our findings show that implementation detail may help agents while making specs prone to decay, that tool-specific record structures shape what people and agents see, and that participants described spec-code checks mainly when changes are completed rather than over time. We also find that individual benefits may come from clarifying intent before delegation, while team benefits may depend on SDD becoming a shared process. We derive implications for tool builders, practitioners, and researchers.

6b4c1d8921aa05591b974b90.title_original: ICON decomposition: Multivariate concept auditing reveals shortcuts that neural networks rely on
6b4c1d8921aa05591b974b90.excerpt: arXiv:2608.26083v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep neural networks often exploit spurious associations, a failure known as shortcut learning. Before deployment, models should therefore be audited for reliance on concepts such as acquisition artifacts and patient demographics. Current methods, including linear probes and concept activation vectors, measure concept reliance by asking whether each concept is decodable from a layer. We show that this framing is misleading: decodability reflects not only concept reliance but also correlations among concepts and the outcome in the auditing dataset. We reframe shortcut auditing as a decomposition of the variance of intermediary representations with Independent Canonical cONcepts (ICON). ICON quantifies the share of a layer's variance explained by each concept conditional on all other concepts and the outcome, and also reports the variance left unexplained. Because ICON explanations are comparable across layers, their trajectories distinguish concepts that drive predictions from those that are merely encoded in the representations. In simulated data with ground truth, ICON recovers concept importance more accurately than seven baselines. In skin-cancer and neuroimaging applications, it separates learned shortcuts from merely correlated concepts, which we confirm with independent validation checks.

f2d7ee78e0902bc338023f68.title_original: INTERVenE: Temporal-Abstraction-Interval Based Transformers for Short-Horizon Medical Event Prediction
f2d7ee78e0902bc338023f68.excerpt: arXiv:2608.29901v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electronic Health Record (EHR) prediction models in the intensive care unit must learn from sparse and irregular measurements while preserving the clinical meaning of time and supporting transparent decision-making. We present INTERVenE, a family of Transformer architectures whose input is an interval-based, knowledge-based temporal abstraction (KBTA), a token stream of named clinical concepts (states, trends, events, contexts) drawn from a curated medical ontology, rather than an unnamed bin index or a raw measurement triplet. This naming layer is what we ask KBTA to do: it makes the model's per-token attributions resolve to clinical concepts by construction. INTERVenE offers two complementary variants: an auto-regressive decoder that generates future abstraction trajectories with a per-step risk readout (localizing \emph{when} and \emph{after which events} risk rises), and a bidirectional encoder for single-pass joint risk and time-to-event prediction. On 57,078 MIMIC-IV admissions, INTERVenE-Enc outperformed GRU-D, STraTS, and KarmaLego, reaching a support-weighted AUPRC of 0.672 ($+0.046$ over the strongest neural baseline, with non-overlapping 95\% bootstrap CIs), AUROC of 0.901, and length-of-stay MAE of 44.4\,h. INTERVenE-Ar complements these predictions with generated abstraction trajectories and evolving risk scores, achieving AUROC of 0.854 and AUPRC of 0.588 under the harder generative readout. An alternativ

3da5809aba3925bb8435bb7f.title_original: Tail-Replay: Escaping the Curse of Linear Attention in Prefix Caching for Hybrid LLMs
3da5809aba3925bb8435bb7f.excerpt: arXiv:2608.30310v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hybrid large language models interleave full-attention layers with linear-attention layers to reduce the cost of long-context inference. This structure complicates prefix caching: full-attention key-value caches are token-addressable, whereas linear-attention layers maintain recurrent states that cannot be rolled back to arbitrary prefix boundaries. Existing hybrid prefix caching methods address this mismatch by storing recurrent-state checkpoints. As a result, token-level matches are directly usable only at positions aligned with stored checkpoints, constraining prefix reuse to a discrete set of boundaries. We present Tail-Replay, a prefix caching mechanism that enables unconstrained token-level prefix reuse in hybrid large language models. The key insight is that linear-attention mechanisms such as Gated DeltaNet can be viewed as a structured, lossy compression of the input prefix: gated recurrent updates progressively attenuate the contributions of earlier inputs. Consequently, the recurrent state of a matched prefix can be well approximated by replaying only a short, recent suffix of that prefix. Tail-Replay exploits this property by caching the exact full-attention key-value cache while omitting recurrent-state checkpoints. On a cache hit, it reconstructs the linear-attention states by replaying a short, recent suffix of the matched prefix. As a result, the reuse boundary is determined by the shared tokens rather

79076b96b904c022bb6dcc24.title_original: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs as Generalist Vision-Language-Action Agents for Drone Control: Commanding, Approaching, Tracking and Searching
79076b96b904c022bb6dcc24.excerpt: arXiv:2609.01404v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to make decisions for drones, but existing evaluations are mostly limited to simulation, to a single drone, and to targets that are visible from the start and do not move. We present DroneCATS, a benchmark in which the MLLM alone controls the drone through four actions, and evaluate ten MLLMs from frontier models to small open models. The benchmark varies target visibility, target motion, scene and simulator, and extends to real drones. Beyond a single drone, it adds a multi-drone suite, where one model drives multiple drones, and a commander + sub-agents suite, where a commander model directs one sub-agent for each of the drones. Across these settings, we find that frontier models achieve the highest success rates, but their latency causes them to lose moving targets, while small open models often do not declare arrival even when they reach the target. Guided by this failure analysis, we fine-tune a 2B model on drone action data synthesized from public RGB-D images; its success rate rises from 0% to 31% in simulation and outperforms the frontier models in real flight. With multiple drones, we find that every zero-shot model succeeds more often as the commander of one sub-agent per drone than when it drives all of them from one context, and that commanding success follows general VLM ability. On real drones, we observe that the results broadly follow those

10efe4288ffe836a1a9e7fc7.title_original: Efficiently Estimating Optimal Hyperparameter Scaling Laws through Power-Law Entropy Search
10efe4288ffe836a1a9e7fc7.excerpt: arXiv:2609.01431v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optimal hyperparameter scaling laws describe how the best hyperparameters for large language model (LLM) training change with model and data scale, enabling practitioners to predict optimal configurations at production scales without expensive large-scale tuning. However, estimating these scaling laws conventionally requires exhaustive grid searches over thousands of training runs, consuming enormous computational resources. We introduce Power-Law Entropy Search (PLES), a computational cost-aware acquisition function built on multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization that efficiently estimates optimal hyperparameter scaling laws through adaptive experimentation. A key innovation in PLES is that it searches for candidates that reduce the overall uncertainty of a scaling law estimate, instead of optimizing a single objective function. At each iteration, PLES selects the candidate configuration that maximally reduces the uncertainty of the scaling law estimates per unit computational cost, naturally favoring informative small-scale experiments. We evaluate PLES on synthetic benchmarks, surrogate models fitted to real LLM training data, and actual LLM pre-training runs. Across all settings, PLES converges to accurate optimal hyperparameter scaling laws using less than one-tenth of the computational budget required by conventional grid search and other baselines.

5545bbf0141807adef09d2c0.title_original: Language Models Can Control Their Own Attention
5545bbf0141807adef09d2c0.excerpt: arXiv:2609.02737v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language models spend most of their attention on a small fraction of context, yet they read the entire KV cache to find the few tokens that matter. If the user asks about a previous detail in a 1M-token conversation, global attention layers must scan the full context to generate each token of the reply. A prominent approach pre-selects relevant tokens via lightweight proxy scores, but this extrinsic scoring still incurs O(N) per step. We take an intrinsic approach motivated by the simple question: wouldn't the model already know which parts of the context are relevant? We introduce Declarative Attention (DA), a protocol that elicits the model to declare where it needs to attend within its chain-of-thought, partitioning generation into three modes: (full context), (a specific region), and (recent output only). The inference engine parses these declarations like tool calls and skips most of the KV cache read. Under zero-shot evaluation across 15 long-context tasks, DA on off-the-shelf models (Gemma-4-31B, Qwen-3.6-27B) reduces total attended tokens per response (45.8%, 19.6%), despite extra decoding steps, with modest accuracy drops (1.40pp, 2.10pp) that shrink with model scale. DA unlocks a new axis of sparse attention, with further potential under training-based methods. Code is available at https://github.com/itsnamgyu/declarative-attention.

7b92b7553c23f1b2f5d48ca2.title_original: RefactorPlatform: An Open-Source Harness for Controlled Evaluation of Repository-Scale Refactoring Agents
7b92b7553c23f1b2f5d48ca2.excerpt: arXiv:2609.04898v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Repository-scale refactoring requires coding agents to propagate a single change across many interdependent files without altering program behavior, yet to our knowledge no existing harness isolates the design choices that determine agent success on this task. We present RefactorPlatform, an open-source evaluation harness that holds the environment fixed and varies each design axis explicitly: model backbone (via OpenRouter and GitHub Copilot CLI), execution regime (baseline, retrieval-augmented, and multi-agent), and prompt specificity. Each run executes in an isolated workspace with live terminal streaming, per-task logging of tokens, diffs, and transcripts, AST-based verification, and exportable telemetry for audit and reproduction. Demonstrating the platform on 100 multi-file RefactorBench tasks across four model families, we illustrate the analyses it supports: AST-aware chunking outperforms naive token-window chunking by 25-30 percentage points (pp) across prompt modes, whereas naive retrieval falls below the retrieval-free baseline; a lean retrieval-augmented single agent (86%) beats the sub-agent configuration we evaluated (66%) on matched tasks with no task passing under delegation that fails under retrieval; and retrieval's accuracy gains absorb its token overhead, leaving cost per successful refactoring unchanged. RefactorPlatform is open-sourced to make refactoring-agent evaluation reproducible and auditabl

c82d6957e56bb4d7034ec4ad.title_original: Training-Free Task Vectors for LLM Behavioral Control
c82d6957e56bb4d7034ec4ad.excerpt: arXiv:2609.09054v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Task vectors enable post-training model editing by identifying semantically meaningful directions in weight space, typically computed as the difference between a fine-tuned model and its pretrained initialization. However, this reliance on fine-tuning makes discovering such directions costly and limits the practicality of post-training model editing. To address this limitation, we introduce Training-Free Task Vectors (TFTVs), a novel method to compute task-vector-like directions without requiring fine-tuning. Our method maps activation steering vectors to rank-one weight-space edits using only forward-pass statistics, while satisfying arithmetic properties that directly support learning via addition, forgetting via subtraction, and the composition of multiple edits. Empirically, we evaluate TFTVs on large language model behavioral control tasks and show that they consistently amplify, suppress, and compose target behaviors while preserving general knowledge and problem-solving skills. We also validate our method against other editing and steering baselines, experimentally demonstrating that TFTVs achieve stronger trait control with better or competitive utility preservation. We hope our work opens new directions for the community in post-training model editing and broader training-free model control. Code is available on the project website: tftv-llm.github.io.

db6f4618830a115ca225164a.title_original: A primer on evaluation methods for large language models in healthcare
db6f4618830a115ca225164a.excerpt: arXiv:2609.14819v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have a growing range of applications in medicine, and their evaluation is critical for ensuring they provide benefit and not harm. This evaluation can be more challenging than traditional machine learning for many reasons, including probabilistic and open-ended outputs, and behavior that shifts with prompt design and accumulated context. This review covers four key areas of LLM evaluation: principles of study design, statistical methods, capability evaluation and clinical application evaluation. Capability evaluation considers different benchmarks, including multiple-choice, agentic and multi-turn benchmarks, alongside operational metrics like token usage and latency. Clinical application evaluation addresses establishing accuracy of free text outputs, such as human review and LLM-as-a-judge, and clinical trial approaches. Across sections, we describe underlying concepts and potential pitfalls, while emphasizing the importance of aligning evaluation methods with the research question. Together, this article aims to provide a pragmatic basis for designing and executing rigorous evaluations of healthcare LLMs.

811df1679bc393ad332efab2.title_original: SoK: Trading Agents or Market Crashers? Dissecting Robustness and Security Failures in Academic Financial LLM Trading Schemes
811df1679bc393ad332efab2.excerpt: arXiv:2609.19705v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents already trade with real capital, yet agent-security research has mostly treated them as generic agents. Trading changes the threat: a compromised agent's orders move prices that other participants act on, and an attacker who profits from a crash can trigger the shock that a non-robust agent mishandles. We present FARSIGHT (Financial Agent Robustness and Security Investigation and Global Holistic Taxonomy), a systematization that rates trading agents on robustness to market stress and on security against source manipulation, agent compromise, and agents acting as attackers. It also checks paper-level ratings against released code. Across 15 academic schemes, none earns full credit on any robustness metric, no paper describes a way to halt trading without waiting for LLM inference, and none combines source provenance with cross-source corroboration. In the code of the 7 open-source schemes, no release enforces a stop-loss or position limit outside the LLM, 4 lack a component that their paper or documentation describes, and 2 run model-written code on the host. The same gaps appear beyond finance. Restating FARSIGHT as a domain-independent threat model, we map them onto agents in healthcare, law, software, and crypto. We then trace how compromised agents spread harm, as worms and as cascades that need no further compromise. At published injection rates per hop, a channel read by ten agent

8bb3f58f684c69be364c3469.title_original: Jev for Scientific Decisions: Evaluating Semantic Choices and Their Consequences
8bb3f58f684c69be364c3469.excerpt: arXiv:2609.24965v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scientific workflows often require choosing among known relations before a deterministic calculation can proceed. Whether observations share a culture, treatment or reference standard can change the scientific meaning of the resulting count or comparison. We evaluate Jev as a semantic decision component using a harness that follows its documented guidance and assigns arithmetic to code. The study compares twelve model configurations on twenty source-grounded Choices across ten scientific cases, each repeated five times. We measure semantic selections, downstream outputs and final claim labels separately. Jev matched five other configurations at complete semantic correctness and achieved the lowest observed median latency among successful responses. Across three comparison models, seven wrong selections on one culture-history question changed downstream counts while preserving the correct final label. These results identify a useful role for Jev in prepared scientific decision tasks and show why evaluating that role requires checking the relations and quantities that a workflow will reuse.

84d81804972d0ddeff7e85be.title_original: KV-streams for Efficient Compaction in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
84d81804972d0ddeff7e85be.excerpt: arXiv:2609.35750v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scaling the horizon of agentic LLMs is bottlenecked by the need to fit ever longer context traces in GPU memory. Context compaction has been the most popular mechanism to alleviate this issue, keeping GPU memory constant for a given trace. Unfortunately, most compaction strategies rely on prefilling the LLM context many times over, hindering training throughput. To alleviate this bottleneck and enable efficient trainable compaction, we propose KV-streams, a plug-and-play strategy compatible with any compaction strategy that substantially increases throughput while showing no evidence of hindering performance. KV-streams enable scalable compaction by streaming the KV cache forward rather than flushing it after each compaction. We show that KV-streams enable three different compaction strategies, achieving a 2.6 to 5x wall-clock speedup in training. Beyond efficiency, we find that the streamed KV cache can act as a recurrent state, carrying forward information that has long since disappeared from the context. Specifically, in a controlled setting we show that, contrary to prior work, RL alone is all that is needed for this behavior to emerge. Overall, we show KV-streams to be an efficient and lightweight plug-and-play addition to any post-training pipeline.

015be06f166d7077854b2863.title_original: Interpretable but Fragile? Robustness of Concept Bottlenecks under Geometric-Semantic Perturbations
015be06f166d7077854b2863.excerpt: arXiv:2609.38625v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) are designed to provide interpretable intermediate representations, yet how such bottlenecks affect robustness remains unclear, with existing studies reporting mixed and sometimes contradictory findings. We argue that these discrepancies arise from conflating different robustness notions and perturbation regimes, rather than from fundamental disagreements about CBMs themselves. To disentangle these factors, we introduce a generator-based evaluation framework that enables controlled comparisons between standard classifiers and CBMs under two distinct perturbation types: continuous geometric perturbations in latent space and discrete semantic interventions in concept space. Within this framework, we evaluate robustness both empirically, via prediction and concept-level sensitivity metrics, and certifiably, using randomized smoothing in latent and concept spaces. Across experiments, we reconcile previously conflicting findings by clarifying when, and in what sense, concept bottlenecks do or do not improve robustness. By further analyzing robustness under varying task conditions, including class semantic similarity and concept vocabulary size, we show that interpretability does not inherently confer robustness. Instead, concept bottlenecks shift where and how sensitivity manifests, revealing a nuanced interpretability robustness trade off that depends critically on the perturbation regime a

cb541a20dcbab0bf963d6119.title_original: LEAP: Learned Block-wise Evidence Retrieval for Long Audio-Video Perception
cb541a20dcbab0bf963d6119.excerpt: arXiv:2609.39938v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hour-scale audio-visual question answering is constrained by a context dilemma: dense whole-recording encoding rapidly exhausts context limits, whereas uniform temporal compression severely dilutes fine-grained acoustic and visual evidence. We introduce LEAP, a framework where the model retrieves its own evidence without placing the whole recording in one context. LEAP divides a recording into fixed-duration blocks, applying a lightweight localization pass to each block to score short candidate windows. The highest-ranked windows are pooled and re-encoded in a single bounded answer pass. Consequently, the answer input and peak context remain independent of the recording duration. By decoupling evidence localization from reasoning, our framework can localize candidate temporal windows over pre-computed transcripts without decoding media frames, while preserving fine-grained visual and non-speech evidence by routing the final answering pass over raw audio-visual streams. LEAP trains both stages: a localization LoRA improves the selected windows, and an answer LoRA improves the answers read from the same windows. The block grid natively supports causal queries, enabling LEAP to support streaming inference without streaming-specific training. Across several AVQA benchmarks, LEAP improves over the Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B baseline by 4.5-16.8%, and transfers to a second omni-modal backbone, MiniCPM-o 4.5, surpassing its published

17ac0ef13718d046ceaf3978.title_original: D-DOIT: Training-free Adaptation of Discrete Diffusion via Doob's h-Transform
17ac0ef13718d046ceaf3978.excerpt: arXiv:2610.04938v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose D-DOIT (Discrete Doob-Oriented Inference-time Transformation), a training-free and efficient adaptation method for discrete diffusion models with generic rewards. D-DOIT formulates adaptation as sampling from a reward-tilted target distribution and realizes this transport through Doob's h-transform of the discrete diffusion reverse kernel, using only reward values rather than reward gradients. Unlike continuous diffusion, masked discrete diffusion samples categorical token-reveal transitions rather than continuous state updates. D-DOIT derives the corresponding discrete Doob's h-transform, which guides sampling by reweighting reverse transition probabilities instead of adding a drift correction. To make this transformation practical, D-DOIT avoids expensive future rollouts. At each guided step, D-DOIT samples candidate next states, uses the model prediction head to complete each candidate into a clean sequence, evaluates each completion with the reward oracle, and resamples the next state with probabilities proportional to the rewards. An optional late-stage best-of-K refinement further improves sample quality by branching trajectories only near the end of denoising, avoiding the $K$-fold cost over the full trajectory. Empirically, across regulatory DNA design and protein inverse folding benchmarks, D-DOIT outperforms training-free guidance baselines. It improves enhancer activity and cell-type specificity w

bedc19a28308b4b0ffb26ff2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.07226v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: ``What are the irreducible conditions that are sufficient to produce an outcome?'' is one of the most common questions that recur across computation and science. Its answers, the minimal sufficient witnesses, are what we mean by explanations, mechanisms and reasons. These problems usually ask for multiple minimal witnesses, yet standard RL methods may reveal only one solution or redundant ones. We formalize this problem as minimal-witness identification and introduce Minimal-Witness Reinforcement Learning (MWRL). MWRL takes the union of the sets certified by successful proposals sampled from the policy and credits each proposal for the coverage the group union would lose without that proposal. This credit assignment, derived directly from the problem definition, unifies the demands for minimality and recovery of alternatives from a single black-box verifier bit. Under this principle, we derive a value iteration planner that recovers the entire family of witnesses and a policy gradient method that can scale to large language models. Across different experimental settings, MWRL recovers most minimal witnesses, while other methods return redundant supersets or a single witness. By making witness families learnable from verifier feedback, MWRL expands the scope of reinforcement learning beyond single-solution optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/TSUITUENYUE/MWRL.

0ee8977c0020ad4f6e037258.title_original: LASER: Latent Space Adjoint Matching for Support-Constrained Entropy-Regularized Offline RL
0ee8977c0020ad4f6e037258.excerpt: arXiv:2610.08989v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy optimization from static datasets without costly online interaction, it remains bottlenecked by the risk of executing out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Recent approaches mitigate this by learning a behavior-cloning policy through flow matching and then performing RL within its constrained latent space. However, naively optimizing the latent policy can easily cause the policy to collapse into a brittle mode or exploit sharp artifacts of the learned critic. In this work, we find that entropy regularization is essential in latent-space RL for addressing these challenges. We introduce LASER, a novel offline RL algorithm that applies latent-space adjoint matching to achieve entropy-regularized latent-space RL with expressive flow policies while avoiding backpropagation through time. Through comprehensive experiments on 40 challenging OGBench tasks with varying dataset qualities, we show that LASER achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, LASER uses fixed method-specific hyperparameters across all tasks and outperforms the evaluated baselines, including those with task- and dataset-specific tuning, which highlights the robust applicability of LASER. Project website: https://mit-realm.github.io/laser/.

facc3b62737a85c7b8109d96.title_original: Forensic Analysis of the HackRF One with PortaPack Mayhem Firmware
facc3b62737a85c7b8109d96.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software-defined radios (SDRs) have become an inexpensive, portable platform for replay attacks, location spoofing and jamming. The HackRF One can operate stand-alone when fitted with a PortaPack interface board running the open-source Mayhem firmware. No peer-reviewed study has addressed the forensic analysis of this device family. This work establishes, at source-code level, where forensically relevant data reside on the microSD card of a device running Mayhem v2.0.1, in which format, when they are written and how they should be interpreted. The methodology is applied to an SD card image that the author acquired from their own device after four months of real use, and every inference is drawn from the image alone. The workflow covers timestamp rules that depend on the real-time clock (RTC) battery state, traces of on-device trimming and text editing, cluster-level recovery of deleted in-phase/quadrature (IQ) captures, and decoding of recorded signals cross-checked with an independent decoder. In the example image, the final part of a deleted IQ capture and a trimmed-away capture segment are recovered, and six captures are attributed to a single rolling-code on-off keying (OOK) transmitter sharing one 32-bit identifier. The study provides practitioners with an artifact catalogue, interpretation rules and acquisition recommendations.

0fc71cefdec76bfc6a97fd10.title_original: Unmasking the Secret Code: Using Canaries to Show How Masked Context Controls Memorization in SFT
0fc71cefdec76bfc6a97fd10.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Canaries, or synthetic training records containing known secrets, are widely used to assess whether language models reveal information from their training data. But how much do these measurements depend on the canaries themselves? We study this question through controlled fine-tuning experiments with language and vision-language models, spanning synthetic tasks and tasks where training improves useful performance. Whether a secret is provided in the training input strongly changes what the model learns; for example, models can reproduce a secret in the input yet fail to recall it when it is removed, even after extensive repetition during training. When training instead requires predicting the secret from the surrounding context, later recall can become reliable. Repetition alone is therefore insufficient to characterize memorization. We also find that changing when a canary appears, or which other canaries accompany it, can substantially change measured memorization without increasing that canary's repetition count. These results show that canary measurements depend on how secrets are presented during training and tested afterward. Audits should test whether their conclusions hold across these choices before extending them to other training records.

04b8baa7d8aba8c2a9cef039.title_original: Empirical Evaluation of Machine Learning for Cloud Cryptojacking Detection: Effects of Preprocessing and Evaluation Protocols
04b8baa7d8aba8c2a9cef039.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied to cloud cryptojacking detection. Classical machine learning models remain among the most widely used approaches for cloud cryptojacking detection. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of six widely used classical machine learning models for AI-based cloud cryptojacking detection under different preprocessing and evaluation settings. Because no public cloud-native cryptojacking dataset is currently available, experiments were conducted using two publicly available proxy datasets, DS2OS and NSL-KDD. The evaluated models include Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, Decision Tree, and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Experimental results show that preprocessing choices and evaluation protocols have a measurable impact on model performance. On DS2OS, removing identifier-related features reduced the accuracy of most models to approximately 96%, while KNN achieved higher accuracy with lower attack recall. On NSL-KDD, models obtained 77 to 80\% accuracy on the official test set containing unseen attack types, compared with above 99.5% under a random train-test split. 0f5b8b9a44c0635a86084e48.title_original: Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network for Interpretable Big Data Analytics and Secure Cloud Decision-Making Systems
0f5b8b9a44c0635a86084e48.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Big data analytics supports modern intelligent systems, but model complexity and limited transparency can undermine interpretability, trust, and security in decision-making. 6ecf05c5ccecc1a5aba2be89.title_original: CascadeLedger: Counterfactual Auditing of Information and Resource Integrity in LLM Cascades
6ecf05c5ccecc1a5aba2be89.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce CascadeLedger, a counterfactual execution-audit framework for budgeted language-model cascades. The central object is aggregate-equivalent trace validity: two executions can share a final answer, declared resource projection, and service histogram while differing in whether their routing decisions used only legitimately observable information. We complement single-trace invariants with counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), which couples a visible prefix and policy randomness while changing only a declared hidden family. 02e509f0e87ddc7da55eab23.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences. A new security abstraction is emerging to fill this void: hardware-software leakage contracts. To support the principled development of secure software on modern hardware such contracts characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level. Thereby they enable programmers and compilers to generate code that is provably resistant to side-channel attacks---without having to explicitly reason about the microarchitecture. On the other hand, they provide a specification for hardware designers to ensure that microarchitectures do not introduce unintended and undocumented side channels. This paper introduces the foundations of this emerging topic, discussing recent contributions and unresolved challenges along the way.

9d3e86b39574cbc11e5a5da6.title_original: Performance Characterization of Pulsar's Software-defined Watermark Verifier
9d3e86b39574cbc11e5a5da6.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pulsar provides the world's most secure PNT service by incorporating a Combinatorial Watermark into its ranging service. 09ef5bbf43f9467415aee124.title_original: GhostLock: Learning-Assisted Blind GPS Signal Nullification Without Victim-Side Information
09ef5bbf43f9467415aee124.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Global Positioning System (GPS) provides critical positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services for numerous safety- and mission-critical applications, making it an attractive target for physical-layer attacks. d59e3a54388a9a3e7e52c978.title_original: Thinking in Graphs: Neo4j-Backed Exploit-Chain Reasoning for LLM Penetration-Testing Agents
d59e3a54388a9a3e7e52c978.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can drive penetration-testing tools, but they reason about an engagement as a flat list of findings in a context window. 23bb23529f571714baf5d93d.title_original: From Detection to Decision: Calibration and Deferral for Prompt-Injection Detection
23bb23529f571714baf5d93d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt-injection defenses are commonly evaluated as binary detectors, although deployed LLM applications must make operational decisions about whether to allow, block, or escalate potentially malicious inputs. 5c8bf49845d608a3ced8fc46.title_original: Does Client Diversity Protect the Lightning Network? Evidence from the 2026 Core Lightning Shutdown

92f0af34175bb03a520fea17.title_original: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
92f0af34175bb03a520fea17.excerpt: arXiv:2610.20962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. 2e4ef57a352470bb58886019.title_original: Can Autonomous Vehicles Keep Their Cool? A Survey of Thermal Side-Channel and Perception Attacks
2e4ef57a352470bb58886019.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) couple safety-critical perception to thermally constrained compute. Interfaces built for night perception and package thermal reliability were never engineered as confidentiality boundaries, and closing one such path leaves the other intact. Physical adversaries can spoof thermal infrared (IR) sensors used for night driving, while unprivileged software co-tenants can fingerprint perception workloads from thermal, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), and thermal event interrupt (TEI) telemetry required for package safety. cd55576702dba0043e28ae19.title_original: NOMAI: Scalable Federated Learning with Private Weights
cd55576702dba0043e28ae19.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21059v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The twin goals of privacy-preserving federated learning (FL) -- harnessing distributed data while protecting the parties who contribute it -- demands three properties: model privacy, data privacy, and integrity. We present NOMAI, the first scalable MPC-based FL system to provide all three guarantees simultaneously. NOMAI operates under an honest-majority assumption in the semi-honest model, with an extension to the malicious-with-abort setting. At its core, NOMAI combines a multi-committee MPC architecture with packed Shamir secret sharing, enabling SIMD-style secure computation that scales far beyond what monolithic n-party protocols can support. 1294ecfdf85dcf74e6d7b594.title_original: Reaction Attack on CKKS Deployments with Asymptotically Optimal Query Complexity
1294ecfdf85dcf74e6d7b594.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a protocol-level reaction leakage in CKKS deployments where public coefficient-to-slot (C2S) evaluation keys are combined with a client's 1-bit validity response. The attack does not break RLWE or CKKS IND-CPA security. Instead, it exploits the interaction between client-side validity reactions and public homomorphic linear transformations. A shift of a public encryption key yields a ciphertext whose plaintext is a function of the secret key; the public ${\sf C2S}$ layer then repacks this information to construct a ciphertext whose validity depends strictly on whether a targeted secret coefficient matches a guessed value. Furthermore, each submitted query is independently randomized with a fresh encryption of zero, so that each resulting malicious ciphertext appears entirely distinct, thereby allowing the attack to simply evade trivial detection mechanisms on the client side. e89ebfb5790a8cba6a350279.title_original: ExecWeave: Cross-Layer Execution Provenance for Observable Agentic Software
e89ebfb5790a8cba6a350279.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic software invokes tools, launches processes, accesses files, and communicates with local or remote services. Application traces describe logical operations, whereas operating-system telemetry records machine activity without necessarily identifying the responsible agent action. Relating these evidence planes is a reconstruction problem: a plausible but unsupported association can assign an effect to the wrong principal. We present ExecWeave, a local-first system that materializes provider semantics and independently observed runtime events into a typed execution graph. The implementation retains separate source artifacts, distinguishes logical occurrences from repeated evidence, and records attribution, inference, and causal-status metadata. An optional command-to-process correlator emits a non-causal inferred bridge only when its bounded search yields one compatible observed process; uniqueness within this observed candidate set is not a guarantee of causal correctness. OS-observed file and network effects acquire a semantic tool or agent principal only through an observed process plus a justified command-to-process association; session-correlated file-system events do not by themselves provide that principal. Source code is available at https://github.com/Irish-kw/ExecWeave.

6591b32b62a7e28c3ddadfb6.title_original: Clean Data Can Still Carry Backdoors: Support-Persistent Backdoors for Model Reuse
6591b32b62a7e28c3ddadfb6.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional backdoor attacks inject artificial trigger patterns into training data, causing models to misclassify triggered inputs while maintaining normal behavior on clean samples. DAR identifies naturally abundant patterns in low-dimensional feature subspaces using subspace clustering and applies label-only poisoning to samples that inherently satisfy the discovered rule. At test time, the backdoor is activated by locally modifying the corresponding subspace of the target images. By instantiating spatial and frequency operators, DAR achieves attack accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art backdoor attacks in ImageNet classification and CLIP-based prompt tuning. 224fe636566562c59cb46b04.title_original: On the Complexity of Symmetric Boolean Functions in Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages
224fe636566562c59cb46b04.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages (PSM), also known as Decomposable Randomized Encoding (DRE) or information-theoretic garbling, is a model for non-interactive secure computation. f2ff4f85a065143d5640b7a1.title_original: From One Query to Many: A Critical Survey of Privacy Accounting in RAG
f2ff4f85a065143d5640b7a1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables large language models to leverage external knowledge but introduces privacy risks when the retrieved corpus contains sensitive information. Differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, yet interpreting and comparing privacy guarantees across existing DP-RAG methods remains challenging. In particular, a privacy budget reported for a single response does not directly characterize privacy loss over repeated queries, and even identical values of $\varepsilon$ may represent different guarantees depending on the protected data unit, accounting horizon, and observable outputs. This survey critically examines how privacy accounting evolves from single-query generation to multi-query RAG systems. We categorize existing approaches into query-time privatization, multi-query accounting, and one-time corpus privatization. We analyze their underlying assumptions and privacy--utility trade-offs. Rather than ranking methods by $\varepsilon$ alone, we propose a framework that interprets a DP-RAG guarantee along three dimensions: privacy granularity, accounting scope, and release boundaries. We conclude that an $\eps$ is a claim only together with the three slots: the protected unit, the accounting scope, and the release boundary.

0f4e45aa15e5c6343de0fe7d.title_original: Trigger Value Selection in Clean-Label Malware Backdoors: An Effectiveness-Detectability Analysis
0f4e45aa15e5c6343de0fe7d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clean-label backdoor poisoning is a threat to machine learning-based malware classifiers because poisoned samples can be inserted into training data without changing their labels. Previous explanation-guided attacks mainly focus on selecting important trigger features, but the values assigned to these features can also affect the attack behavior. In this paper, we study trigger value selection as an independent design factor in clean-label backdoor attacks against feature-based malware classifiers. We evaluate several value-selection strategies on EMBER 2018 and a Win64 PE subset of EMBER 2024 using LightGBM classifiers. We compare rare-value, SHAP-based, frequency-bounded, co-occurrence-aware, and quantile-based selectors under random and distribution-based malware-similar benign sampling. The results show that aggressive selectors such as MinPopulation and CountAbsSHAP can achieve high attack success rate, especially under distribution-based sampling, but they are also easier to detect by sanitization methods such as Isolation Forest. These findings show that trigger value selection is not merely an implementation detail, but an important design choice that shapes the effectiveness and detectability profile of clean-label malware backdoor attacks.

59ee09b2ad8de274a2f28b61.title_original: When Rotation Bounds Nothing: Streaming Image Classifiers to Field Nodes Under Physical Capture
59ee09b2ad8de274a2f28b61.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Field nodes run image classifiers locally, exposing a first-class asset, the trained model, to theft. Here the operator owns the node, and an adversary seizing it reads only what cold-boot capture finds resident. One answer stores nothing: a chunkable multi-exit model streams into volatile memory, rotating to bound residency. We characterise the capture envelope on real LTE traces across two victims of one architecture, against passive and adaptive adversaries. Neither survives a capable adversary; recovery cost alone differs. Against a from-scratch victim the uncaptured stages must be learned: the adaptive adversary gains most at shallow seizures, ends the CIFAR-10 envelope at every rotation, and stays rotation-bounded on CIFAR100, from 42.6% of usable seizures at 5 s to 86.8% at 30 s. Against the same architecture sliced from a public pretrained backbone, the adversary downloads those stages, recovering at least 90% of maximum accuracy at all depths, taking usable CIFAR-100 seizures from 0.0% to 97.3% at 5 s, given the victim's full labelled training set. a63021c987b4032ff7895090.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21309v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools help detect potential software vulnerabilities, but they themselves contain faults undermining reliability and usability. Our key insight is leveraging LLMs to understand and transform code in diverse programming languages. We design novel metamorphic relations with transformations to guide variant generation, using an LLM to produce multi-language variants that satisfy these relations. To reduce erroneous variants and identify unique faults, we propose two heuristics: dynamic-feedback-driven selection and program-differencing-based clustering. LLM4SAST identified 66 unique faults across six SAST tools, with 32 confirmed or fixed after being reported to developers, demonstrating effectiveness. 3fa30c7f06b2e6051ff06ea1.title_original: Evaluating and Improving Static Application Security Testing Tools for Rust
3fa30c7f06b2e6051ff06ea1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rust has become a popular systems programming language in recent years because of its strong guarantees on memory and concurrency safety. Many types of system software have been re-implemented in Rust. However, Rust programs can still suffer from common memory and concurrency vulnerabilities due to unsafe code and misunderstandings of its complex mechanisms. To mitigate such vulnerabilities, developers often rely on static application security testing (SAST) tools. However, the effectiveness of existing Rust SAST tools on real-world vulnerabilities remains underexplored. In this paper, we first conduct an empirical evaluation of mainstream Rust SAST tools using security vulnerabilities identified in real-world Rust applications. We systematically assess their effectiveness, uncover common weaknesses, and analyze the root causes behind them. Motivated by the study, we propose TRUST, a large language model (LLM)-assisted automated testing framework. TRUST automatically analyzes the official Rust reference to derive and implement semantics-preserving transformations. It leverages these transformations to generate mutant programs for evaluating Rust SAST tools and uncovering potential faults within them.
