87150cffbefcc437a25aad69.title_original: Cryptographically Secure Agent-to-Agent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
87150cffbefcc437a25aad69.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23078v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) comprise AI agents that collaborate or compete to perform complex, distributed tasks. Their dynamic interactions create opportunities for threat actors to target and impersonate other agents, intercept messages, inject malicious prompts, and exfiltrate sensitive data while simultaneously complicating the detection of anomalous behavior through conventional monitoring. This paper surveys threats and cryptographic challenges in agent-to-agent communication and presents a zero-trust architecture integrating identity, transport security, message integrity, and monitoring. The architecture establishes agent identities via decentralized identifiers and task-scoped verifiable credentials backed by a permissioned ledger, enforcing least-privilege authorization. For transport security, it provides mutually authenticated, crypto-agile TLS with hybrid post-quantum key establishment, and evaluates KEMTLS with pre-distributed public keys to reduce handshake overhead. Signed CBOR envelopes preserve payload integrity across multi-hop exchanges, while zero-knowledge proofs verify declared task constraints without exposing underlying inputs. Context-aware monitoring of inter-agent messages, tool activity, and execution telemetry informs the setting of risk-based trust thresholds and supports the detection of behavioral anomalies. Together, these mechanisms provide an integrated framework for securing and auditing agent

dc176e5d02f66ff5f7b591c5.title_original: Trojan Horse: Automated Repository Poisoning against Coding Agents
dc176e5d02f66ff5f7b591c5.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents are increasingly capable with autonomy, which exposes them to repository-level poisoning. Existing red-teaming studies remain restricted to manual selection for malicious payload locations and fixed disguise strategies, which cannot represent realistic repository poisoning. We present TrojanForge, the first automated framework for repository poisoning. TrojanForge parses repository structure through abstract syntax trees (AST) and maps agent execution traces onto AST nodes. A security review agent ranks these candidates and selects the least conspicuous ones for payload mounting. Then, through adversarial play with the target agent, TrojanForge iteratively refines disguise strategies by inverting the causes of agent detection, and transfers accumulated success experience across repositories. We further construct TrojanBench, a benchmark of 384 poisoned repositories spanning 6 domains and 9 programming languages. Extensive experiments show that TrojanForge achieves a stable poisoning success rate of over 60% with backdoor injection exceeding 90%. Comprehensive evaluation on TrojanBench across 4 harnesses and 12 models reveals that even commercial agents fail to defend against repository-level poisoning.

1088429d8e16955e5f6027ed.title_original: AgentLoupe: Kernel-Resident Semantic Causal Labels for AI Agent Observability
1088429d8e16955e5f6027ed.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents translate user intents into system actions via tool invocations. Accurately attributing these actions to their originating LLM interactions is essential for security auditing, yet existing methods, such as AgentSight, fail for delayed execution and cross-process-lineage behaviors. We present AgentLoupe, an application-transparent eBPF-based observability tool. The core insight of AgentLoupe is to embed causal identity into kernel resources.AgentLoupe employs eBPF to capture TLS plaintext to interpret LLM interactions, and assigns each a kernel-resident semantic label.It maintains labels in eBPF maps, then propagates this label across processes and threads, associates it with kernel resources such as files and sockets. When a persistent resource carries context to an independent process outside the original lineage, this design preserves the delayed causal association.Experiments show that the average observation overhead of AgentLoupe is below 8%, and case studies confirm AgentLoupe traces cross-lineage persistent attacks back to their originating LLM interactions.

4de25fb1280f901634aa5bb8.title_original: MobileJailBench: Red Queen Jailbreak Benchmarking for Mobile Agents
4de25fb1280f901634aa5bb8.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: MLLM-based mobile agents are rapidly gaining autonomy in perception, planning, and closed-loop execution in dynamic mobile environments. However, this autonomy also broadens the attack surface and amplifies the risks of malicious misuse, including privacy leakage, device compromise, and large-scale phishing. Existing jailbreak evaluations leave three critical gaps for mobile agents: they focus on conversational attacks instead of mobile workflows, use static task sets with fixed difficulty, and rely narrowly on attack success rate rather than comprehensive security assessment. To close these gaps, we present MobileJailBench, the first evolving jailbreak benchmark for mobile agents, comprising three key components: (1) a benchmark comprising 520 tasks spanning three jailbreak paradigms and 14 risk categories, built on a high-fidelity mobile sandbox that we construct, enabling realistic workflows across over 20 widely used apps; (2) Dual-Dynamic Evolution, which combines Failure-Distilled Jailbreak Evolution with Weakness-Driven Benchmark Expansion; and (3) Stratified Adjudication Framework for assessing security awareness, execution behavior, and risk consequences. Extensive experiments show that current mobile agents are particularly vulnerable to implicit jailbreaks, as their safety alignment remains largely superficial and fails to generalize from conversational refusal to dynamic mobile interactions. 6cbebe9369c7c0a0cefd8eb2.title_original: On the (In)stability of Adaptive Fee Mechanisms in Multi-Chain Systems
6cbebe9369c7c0a0cefd8eb2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EIP-1559 has become the dominant transaction fee mechanism in permissionless blockchains, regulating scarce block space through an adaptive base fee. The design balances a trade-off between responsiveness to demand fluctuations and stability of long-term resource usage. On a single chain, this trade-off is well understood and empirically stable. In multi-chain systems, however, cross-chain flows introduce delayed economic interactions across otherwise independent fee markets. These interactions alter the control dynamics and create stability risks that existing models do not capture. Deployed systems have already polarized. Polkadot enforces conservative update rates, effectively disabling fee adaptivity and reverting the market to inefficient first-price auctions. Cosmos adopts aggressive update rates without formal guarantees. To fill this gap, we propose a control-theoretic framework that formalizes multi-chain fee markets as a nonlinear dynamical system with delayed feedback. We identify delay-amplified over-correction as the structural root of instability. Experiments show that cross-chain coupling erodes stability relative to monolithic blockchains, reducing the safe parameter space for base fee update rates by up to 84.8%. Moreover, instability propagates across chains, contaminating the otherwise stable peer chains. 1308f46db78fbfac3df5b45c.title_original: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection
1308f46db78fbfac3df5b45c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based mobile agents are rapidly evolving from conversational assistants into autonomous systems that perceive, reason over, and act on smartphone environments. This capability also exposes a new security risk: adversaries can embed malicious objectives in cross-application mobile content and steer agent behavior through indirect multimodal injection. Although prompt injection has been studied in desktop and web settings, its cross-modal properties in mobile ecosystems remain poorly understood, and existing security analyses are still limited. To close this gap, we introduce MobileInject, the first benchmark for evaluating mobile agents against multimodal injection attacks and reasoning-to-action security risks. MobileInject provides a high-fidelity interactive mobile evaluation framework covering 11 scenarios, 9 security-risk categories, and 108 executable risk instances. It further introduces Cross-Modal Consistency Injection to exploit corroboration across modalities, two enhanced attack methods, Multi-Role Collaborative Deception and Reasoning-Camouflage Injection, to intensify trust manipulation and reasoning hijacking, and a Reasoning Security Diagnosis Framework for fine-grained failure analysis. 37f7c86e8e452a8c03687580.title_original: From Billion-Scale to Million-Scale Language Models: Operational Capabilities for Embedded Post-Exploitation
37f7c86e8e452a8c03687580.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for resource-constrained environments due to their low computational footprint. These characteristics also make them candidates for future autonomous malware, where connectivity, latency, privacy, or operational constraints may preclude cloud-based inference. Yet the ability of ultra-compact models to support malware during post-exploitation remains poorly understood. We systematically evaluate seven open-source SLMs (20M-1.5B parameters) on two post-exploitation code-generation tasks: Directory Enumeration and Backdoor Generation. We compare Python (high-resource) and Lua (low-resource) across prompting strategies, task formulations, iterative reasoning, grammar-constrained decoding, and execution-feedback loops. Results show that offensive code-generation capabilities do not increase linearly with model size. Successful execution depends on the interaction of model capacity, task formulation, and prompting strategy, with task formulation exerting a greater influence than prompt engineering alone. Algorithmic formulation combined with few-shot prompting enables Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B to reach Pass@5 of 100% in both Python and Lua for Directory Enumeration, 100% in Python for Backdoor Generation, and 99.2% in Lua. Although the evaluated models remain too computationally demanding for widespread deployment in contemporary malware, rapid progress in compact models may reduce thi

94617774ee066ff8ba1d4a69.title_original: Token-Level Attribution of Multi-Mode LLM Watermarks: Optimal Rule and Belief Weighting
94617774ee066ff8ba1d4a69.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A watermark verifier may hold many modes, i.e., secret keys, and a document may mix spans of different modes with unwatermarked text. Directly reporting the mode with the largest pivotal statistic (pivot) inflates the Type I error, and restoring the nominal level reduces power as candidate modes are added. We formulate token-level multi-mode attribution for the Gumbel-max watermark as maximizing correct-label power under a Type I error constraint given a mode prior. We show that the optimal rule reports the mode with the largest prior-weighted alternative density and rejects when this density exceeds one common threshold. Based on this rule, we propose the Belief-weighted Likelihood Attribution with Density Estimation (BLADE) detector. It estimates the mode prior from neighboring pivots and the alternative density from reference token probabilities. Under a conditional product model of the pivots, it keeps the exact Type I error. We further show that BLADE approaches the optimal rule as its prior and density estimates improve, with a sharp coefficient on the density error. On OPT-1.3B and other open-weight large language models, BLADE attains higher correct-label power than the compared detectors across candidate counts, token-substitution rates, generation temperatures and generator models.

4dea399cc8d41bb7e255649c.title_original: ABF-Bench: A Verifiable Benchmark for Agentic Blockchain Forensics
4dea399cc8d41bb7e255649c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blockchain forensics is adversarial and open-ended: money launderers split, swap, and bridge funds, cut their trail at mixers or custodial services, and change tactics from one incident to the next. Investigators must keep adapting their tracing in response. Yet the immutability of public ledgers preserves every recorded movement in public view, making much of the investigation independently verifiable. We introduce ABF-Bench, an interactive benchmark that makes evidence-backed fund tracing a verifiable agent task, in which every claimed movement must cite ledger records the agent retrieved. A case-to-task pipeline builds well-posed tasks across ledgers: conservative rules halt tracing wherever the records leave a continuation unresolved, and each task's reference graph is the answer those rules determine. Built from real laundering activity, the tasks combine multi-hop transfers, DeFi exchanges, cross-chain round trips, custodial and mixer deposits, and address poisoning. We also propose the ABF agent harness, built around a working memory, and evaluate it alongside general-purpose agents and fixed-order tracers. The harness reaches 75% edge recall, against 47% for Codex with the same model and 10% for Claude Code, which loses recall to overconfidence: it cites records it left unretrieved. Compared with fixed-order tracers, the harness acquires evidence faster than the best of them early in the budget and recognizes undisclosed

306fbc1a9dfbee63f0828e6f.title_original: TUPLE-Bench: Evaluating and Mitigating Privacy-Utility Trade-offs in Typed Decision Models
306fbc1a9dfbee63f0828e6f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed decision models often return more than a selected category. They also expose probabilities for each candidate and, sometimes, a separate confidence score. These fields support downstream decisions but may reveal information beyond a recipient's authorization. We introduce TUPLE-Bench (Typed decision models' Utility and Privacy Leakage Evaluation Benchmark), a benchmark of paired synthetic cases in which recipients may learn a coarse operational category but not its fine-grained cause. Across nine models, instructions to withhold the cause fail to protect it: 91.88%-99.93% of responses reveal the cause through direct selection or residual scores. Even when causes are excluded from the candidate set, full outputs enable 62.85%-75.35% recovery on held-out cases, compared with 51.04%-57.64% using only the selected category (50% chance). Full outputs also reduce mean downstream cost in all 27 model-task comparisons. However, confidence fields increase leakage without consistently reducing cost. We further introduce workflow-constrained privacy quantization (WCPQ), which reduces secret recovery while preserving the behavior and cost of specified downstream workflows. Our findings highlight the need to audit decision interfaces field by field and workflow by workflow.

8d09eeadda8e82ba3b83f6b3.title_original: HardEval: An Execution-Verified Benchmark for AI-Driven Security Hardening and Compliance Remediation
8d09eeadda8e82ba3b83f6b3.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Implementing Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) controls remains a demanding operating-system administration task. Each natural-language security requirement must be translated into a precise and persistent configuration change. These changes span Secure Shell (SSH) configuration, authentication policy, audit rules, and kernel parameters. Existing benchmarks do not measure whether a model can perform this task on a live system. Code benchmarks evaluate isolated programs without persistent system state, while agent benchmarks largely focus on applications rather than operating-system configuration. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{HardEval}, an execution-verified benchmark for evaluating language-model-assisted security hardening. HardEval is built from Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 STIG controls that fail on an unhardened baseline system. Expert-written reference remediations and Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL) checks serve as hidden ground truth for grading; they are never shown to the model, and each task states only the required security outcome while withholding the implementation. The model produces a Bash script, which is executed on a live virtual machine and graded from fail to pass using the corresponding OpenSCAP/OVAL compliance check. Evaluation of fourteen frontier and open-weight configurations reveals large and uneven capability differences across security domains. A recurring failure

3f1676f2d46c7180295ba799.title_original: RedDarwin: Evolving Jailbreak Skills against Frontier LLMs
3f1676f2d46c7180295ba799.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Red teaming must continually adapt as frontier LLM safeguards evolve, yet existing approaches largely search for adversarial prompts or optimize within fixed attack procedures. We observe that even when an attack becomes ineffective, its underlying mechanisms can remain useful and can be revised or recombined to construct stronger attacks. Based on this insight, we introduce RedDarwin, an agentic framework that shifts the unit of jailbreak evolution from prompts and fixed attacks to executable attack skills. RedDarwin consists of 47 reusable base skills and autonomously revises, composes, executes, and selects them using target-model feedback, allowing successful discoveries to become building blocks for subsequent evolution. RedDarwin produces 65 evolved skills, improving 44 of 47 base attacks and increasing their mean attack success rate (ASR) on AdvBench from 18.8% to 47.3%. These evolved skills consistently outperform baselines on the held-out StrongREJECT and frontier LLMs unseen during evolution; with only 10 target-model queries, RedDarwin achieves 100% ASR on GPT-5.6-Sol, 92% on Claude-Sonnet-5, and 80% on Gemini-3.8-Flash. Analysis of the evolution trajectories further shows that strong attacks often emerge from novel combinations of reusable mechanisms rather than from individually dominant ones. We believe this paradigm can accelerate adaptive red teaming and inform stronger safeguards, creating complementary value fo

04cc1fe7a6c880a5a73c6936.title_original: Broad and Efficient PII Detection with Unified Labels
04cc1fe7a6c880a5a73c6936.excerpt: arXiv:2610.22597v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection models must efficiently find identifiers across diverse contexts while maintaining a low false-positive rate (FPR) on high-volume traffic. Recent detectors increasingly rely on complex architectures that raise deployment cost, yet many are fine-tuned on only a few synthetic datasets that limit their coverage. Combining public datasets is challenging because their taxonomies differ, and even after categories are mapped to a common schema, labels can disagree on what counts as a detection, producing inconsistent training and evaluation signals. To address these problems, we present a practical 141M-parameter encoder-based detector trained on 1.12 million examples from 77 public datasets, relabeled under a detailed definition of broad contextual detection for 12 structured PII categories. Evaluated on the AI4Privacy and Nemotron-PII benchmarks at a low-FPR operating point, our model achieves the highest recall against larger baselines in 11 of 14 comparisons under our labels and 9 of 14 under the original labels. Its largest recall gains include useful additional coverage, such as multilingual disclosures and IP addresses embedded in URLs. It achieves this with 2-10x higher throughput and 94-97% less peak GPU memory than the baselines, delivering leading detection performance at substantially lower cost.

a22b78b858dd019662bb1c50.title_original: Watermarkability: Measuring and Improving Language-Model Compatibility with Logit-Based Watermarks
a22b78b858dd019662bb1c50.excerpt: arXiv:2610.22810v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language-model watermarks can help identify model-generated text, encode provenance information, and detect post-generation edits. A broad class of logit-based watermarks increases the logits of a designated token set at each decoding step. Because a base model's native probability mass on this set varies across contexts, models, and watermark rules, the same logit bias can yield different adherence rates and increases in perplexity (PPL). We introduce watermarkability to characterize the compatibility between a model and the token sets requested by a watermark. At a target mass $\tau$, we quantify this property through a watermarkability cost: the expected minimum KL divergence from the base-model distribution required to assign probability at least $\tau$ to the requested set. A lower cost means that the model is more watermarkable for that request distribution. To reduce this cost, we propose a two-stage method. In the first stage, we train a target-set-conditioned low-rank adapter on unions drawn from a 16-way vocabulary partition to increase the requested set's probability mass. In the second stage, a closed-form controller applies the smallest remaining uniform logit bias needed to reach the target mass. We evaluate the method on six watermark schedules using OPT-125M and Qwen3-8B. Across the 12 model-schedule pairs, the pre-adaptation watermarkability cost correlates with the log-PPL increase under a near-hard fixed-bia

66238063a9daeecd6ae87d05.title_original: Identify, Classify, Act: Per-Instruction Controlled Compliance for LLMs over External Data
66238063a9daeecd6ae87d05.excerpt: arXiv:2610.22874v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLMs over external data face a per-instruction tension: a single document or tool return often interleaves legitimate directives with adversarial prompt injections, and the model must follow the former while rejecting the latter. Existing defenses suppress or trust all external instructions, collapsing the safety-utility frontier and forcing a choice between over-refusal and over-compliance. We argue the missing capability is \textbf{per-instruction credit attribution} and formalize it as External-Data Instruction Classification, an identify-classify-act decision over each embedded directive. We propose \textbf{EDIC}, a decomposed reward framework for per-instruction compliance. A scene-grounded pipeline injects mixed beneficial and harmful instructions with counterfactual filtering, while a generative judge is initialized by SFT and refined with GRPO to attribute compliance at the instruction level. The judge then produces a reward that separately encourages beneficial compliance and penalizes harmful compliance for RL training. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, EDIC improves both safety and utility over the strongest prior defense, lifting harmful-rejection by up to 7.7\% and Arena-Hard-Auto utility by 12.5\% on Qwen3-4B. The code repository is hosted at https://github.com/yingyingxia666/EDIC.

e05d4ce27dba8f964eaa524f.title_original: Towards Hyperparameter Transfer for Differentially Private Optimization
e05d4ce27dba8f964eaa524f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.22976v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scaling laws and hyperparameter tuning remain central challenges in training large-scale models, particularly under differential privacy (DP), where optimization is further complicated by noise injection and per-sample gradient clipping. While Maximal Update Parametrization ($\mu$P) allows for zero-shot hyperparameter transfer in standard training, we show that it fails under DP constraints due to the distinct spectral properties of high-dimensional noise versus low-rank gradients. In this work, we introduce DP-$\mu$P, a theoretically grounded framework that extends $\mu$P to the privacy-preserving setting. By analyzing the interaction between gradient clipping, noise injection, and feature learning, we derive a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) condition that governs layer-wise learning rate scaling. Combining this with our proposed spectral scaling formulation, we provide specific scaling rules for DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon optimizers. Empirically, we demonstrate that DP-$\mu$P enables effective zero-shot transfer of learning rates across model widths on diverse architectures (MLP, ViT, GPT-2), matching or exceeding the performance of individually tuned baselines while significantly reducing computational costs.

8ba2bcfab26d6254f9a34051.title_original: VulnSAGE: Adjudicating SAST Reports by Connecting LLM Reasoning to Program Structure
8ba2bcfab26d6254f9a34051.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23035v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) reports flag operations whose safety depends on project-specific context, and maintainers must decide which reports describe real defects. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret this context, but adjudicating a report with them requires the decisive code, which often lies far from the reported line, and a decision basis that program analysis can check. We present VulnSAGE, an adjudication system for SAST reports that connects LLM reasoning to program structure in both directions. Its report-centered slicer recovers the dependencies of the reported operation together with the program structure that explains them, such as the caller object on which a helper acts. CLAIM, an intermediate representation for report judgments, records each model interpretation as a semantic fact that cites the program relations it assumes. Program analysis checks these premises, and the verdict follows from the facts whose premises hold. Both mechanisms share a program graph, which lets the model cite the code it reads and lets the checker query those citations. Statically supported true positives then guide proof-of-concept generation and runtime reproduction. Across 187 labeled reports from four corpora covering five vulnerability families, VulnSAGE rejects 89 of 97 false alarms and retains 85 of 90 real defects. Under a common PoC procedure, 25 of its positive verdicts reproduce at runtime, compared w

f45687079023012b847bac82.title_original: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
f45687079023012b847bac82.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood. For three-party equality on $n$-bit inputs, which determines whether the players' $n$-bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication $(1.633\ldots)n$ qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least $3n$ qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication $3\log_2 3$. Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every $k\geq 3$, we construct a perf

9ddc6fc7f21401468357a4d5.title_original: From GAN-Based Models to GPT-5: A Taxonomy-Guided Study of Human Performance in Detecting Deepfake Face Images
9ddc6fc7f21401468357a4d5.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23144v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative models for deepfakes have rapidly evolved from GAN-based architectures to diffusion models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, empirical research on human performance in detecting deepfake face images has not kept pace. It remains unclear if (and how) detection performance varies across generative models and whether model-specific training improves detection more effectively than general-purpose training. In this paper, we propose the \emph{Deepfake Face Artifact Taxonomy} (DFAT), a cross-model taxonomy of human-recognizable visual artifacts in deepfake face images, based on which we build both general-purpose and model-specific training materials. Through an online experiment ($n = 524$), we examined human performance in detecting deepfake face images and evaluated training efficacy across five representative generative models: three GAN-based, one diffusion-based, and one MLLM (GPT-5). Our results show that participants' detection accuracy was strongly model-dependent and that images generated by more recent and advanced models were not necessarily harder to detect. After training, participants achieved significant performance gains across most conditions, and their improvement varied by model. Notably, model-specific training generally yielded greater numerical gains than general-purpose training. In a five-month follow-up test ($n = 342$), we observed no significant decline in detection accura

a39a0f5cdbd2ed0796f54510.title_original: Ignored, Not Refused: What Low Prompt-Injection Success Rates Hide in Small Tool-Using Agents
a39a0f5cdbd2ed0796f54510.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23254v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tool-using agents read untrusted external content, which exposes them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where hidden instructions hijack the agent's tool calls. Benchmarks measure IPI security by the attack success rate (ASR), which treats every failed attack as a successful defense. To test this assumption, we audit 33,000 trajectories from eleven open-weight agents (2-14B parameters) on InjecAgent and AgentDojo. A label-blind LLM judge shows that most failed attacks are ignored (76-80%) rather than refused (17-18%). With identical model weights, changing only the system prompt shifts InjecAgent ASR from 0.2% to 43%. Our Attack-Task Outcome Matrix (ATOM) further shows that in 21.7% of AgentDojo episodes, the agent stayed safe but did not complete the user's task. A low ASR therefore mostly reflects agents silently ignoring injections, not refusing them. Evaluations should report how attacks fail and whether the user's task is completed, alongside ASR. We release the labeled corpus, judge prompt, and analysis code.

c4d69324469a51df6504f993.title_original: Monitor-Validity Failures: LLM Safety Evidence Paths at Evolving Framework Boundaries
c4d69324469a51df6504f993.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23362v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern LLM applications rely on runtime monitors that inspect tool calls, traces, streams, detector outputs, and verifier inputs. This creates an interface-reliability problem: a framework path may remain operational while policy-relevant evidence never reaches its decision point. In one representative case, a regex detector returned a positive match, but the framework stranded the result before the block decision. This differs from jailbreaks and detector errors because the evidence is already recognized yet disconnected from enforcement. We study this repair-boundary signature with canary contracts: parent/fixed confirmation units that place a known payload only on the changed evidence surface and record monitor visibility together with the downstream decision for action-boundary cases. Applying the protocol to public framework repairs, we confirm 18 evidence-path failures across 11 LLM or agent safety project groups and four implementation ecosystems. Nine are established-boundary repairs, eight are new-surface policy-coverage gaps, and one is a boundary-only evidence case. Fourteen reach E1 enforcement boundaries: seven native action outcomes, six configured enforcement boundaries, and one synthetic-consumer consequence. The remaining cases affect verifier, safety-prompt, or observability channels. The cases form carrier, adapter, authority, and surface families and show how ordinary application behavior can remain intact

40f8ae1ab10ab993cfed1d0a.title_original: Task-aware Kernel Stein certificates for R\'{e}nyi differential privacy
40f8ae1ab10ab993cfed1d0a.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23798v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: R\`enyi differential privacy, based on R\`enyi divergence, has become a notion of choice for privacy guarantees. However, outside the Gaussian setting, R\`enyi divergence can be difficult to compute. In particular, R\`enyi differential privacy guarantees that exploit task-specific information, as in R\`enyi Pufferfish privacy, can be challenging. Here we use kernel Stein discrepancies based on escort distributions to provide certificates for R\`enyi differential privacy. By designing the kernel to focus on the relevant privacy directions, we also derive task-aware privacy certificates. We provide exact identities for Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms and bounds for exponential mechanisms, with separate task-aware guarantees. A real data set example illustrates how the protected comparison set and the released subspace jointly determine the resulting certificates.

e5c44eadbdb685bd39044214.title_original: Bad Diagnosis: Analyzing Consent and Data Collection Practices of Mobile Medical Apps
e5c44eadbdb685bd39044214.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23851v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mobile health (mHealth) apps collect personally-identifiable information while handling uniquely sensitive medical data, ranging from mental health records to real-time glucose or heart rate monitoring -- yet they remain poorly understood at scale. We present the first comprehensive analysis of consent and data collection practices across 10,000+ mHealth apps on the Google Play Store, combining static analysis and privacy policy examination. We develop a rigorous operational definition to distinguish health apps from general wellness programs, and design a measurement framework to detect misuse of permissions and violations of consent. Our analyses reveal a troubling ecosystem: 69.15% of apps request at least one permission unrelated to their stated purpose, with over 52.9% apps requesting location data, and 50.5% and 34.9% apps requesting camera and microphone access, respectively -- despite no functional justification based on app descriptions and stated purposes. Most alarmingly, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, directly violating regulatory requirements such as GDPR; and even among the remaining 7%, 1 in 14 demonstrate a gap between the obtained consent and collection of personally identifiable information. These findings demonstrate an urgent need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mHealth apps. We plan to release our dataset and measurement tools for continued monitoring of th

e9551fd2c077d9ba280eb7d1.title_original: Beyond Boundaries: A Comprehensive Survey of Transferable Attacks on AI Systems
e9551fd2c077d9ba280eb7d1.excerpt: arXiv:2311.11796v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transferable attacks allow adversarial manipulations or learned attack mechanisms constructed in one setting to compromise other AI systems, potentially reducing attack costs and amplifying security and privacy risks. Yet fragmented terminology and evaluation practices hinder understanding of what transfers, why it transfers, and where transfer fails. This survey synthesizes representative research and develops a unified taxonomy spanning six complementary axes: cross-instance, cross-domain, cross-modality, cross-model, cross-task, and cross-deployment. By separating source-target configuration changes from attacker access and adaptation budgets, the taxonomy provides a common framework for comparing transfer across evasion, poisoning, backdoors, privacy inference, model stealing, and prompt-based attacks. We connect transfer mechanisms, including gradient alignment, shared representations, training persistence, and deployment invariances, to enhancement methods based on augmentation, disentanglement, and optimization. Our synthesis identifies inconsistent transfer, incompatible metrics, and gaps between simulated and physical evaluations, and establishes a research agenda for compositional transfer, configuration differences, temporal persistence, and reproducible benchmarking. Together, this work supports systematic investigation of shared vulnerabilities and guides transfer-aware security assessment and defense.

06cf77263d5b8645b0268f13.title_original: A Gradient-Optimized TSK Fuzzy Framework for Explainable Phishing Detection
06cf77263d5b8645b0268f13.excerpt: arXiv:2504.18636v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Phishing attacks represent an increasingly sophisticated and pervasive threat to individuals and organizations, causing significant financial losses, identity theft, and severe damage to institutional reputations. Existing phishing detection methods often struggle to simultaneously achieve high accuracy and explainability, either failing to detect novel attacks or operating as opaque black-box models. To address this critical gap, we propose a novel phishing URL detection system based on a first-order Takagi-Sugeno-Kang (TSK) fuzzy inference model optimized through gradient-based techniques. Our approach intelligently combines the interpretability and human-like reasoning capabilities of fuzzy logic with the precision and adaptability provided by gradient optimization methods, specifically leveraging the Adam optimizer for efficient parameter tuning. Experiments conducted using a comprehensive dataset of over 235,000 URLs demonstrate rapid convergence, exceptional predictive performance (accuracy averaging 99.95% across 5 cross-validation folds, with a perfect AUC i.e. 1.00). Furthermore, optimized fuzzy rules and membership functions improve interoperability, clearly indicating how the model makes decisions - an essential feature for cybersecurity applications. This high-performance, transparent, and interpretable phishing detection framework significantly advances current cybersecurity defenses, providing practitioners wit

d8dc7bb6224431b71a64fd99.title_original: Practical and Private Hybrid ML Inference with Fully Homomorphic Encryption
d8dc7bb6224431b71a64fd99.excerpt: arXiv:2509.01253v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In contemporary cloud-based services, protecting users' sensitive data and ensuring the confidentiality of the server's model are critical. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables inference directly on encrypted inputs, but its practicality is hindered by expensive bootstrapping and inefficient approximations of non-linear activations. We introduce Safhire, a hybrid inference framework that executes linear layers under encryption on the server while offloading non- linearities to the client in plaintext. This design eliminates bootstrapping, supports exact activations, and significantly reduces computation cost. To safeguard model confidentiality despite client access to intermediate outputs, Safhire applies randomized shuffling, which obfuscates intermediate values and makes it practically impossible for a client to reconstruct the model. To further reduce inference latency, Safhire incorporates advanced optimizations such as fast ciphertext packing and partial extraction. Evaluations on multiple standard models and datasets show that Safhire achieves up to 7.6x and 7.4x lower inference latency than Orion and Concrete-ML, respectively, which are two state-of-the-art FHE baselines, with manageable communication overhead and comparable accuracy. These results underline the practicality of our hybrid FHE inference scheme.

8055e4bdf62b4046c274c82f.title_original: OTS-PC: OTS-based Payment Channels for the Lightning Network
8055e4bdf62b4046c274c82f.excerpt: arXiv:2511.04021v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a new type of bidirectional payment channel based on One-Time Signatures on state sequence numbers. This new construction is simpler than the Poon-Dryja construction, but provides a number of benefits such as $O(1)$ storage per channel, minimal information leakage, and compatibility with Lightning Network routing.

e04973bf5f0ed53bf288ff40.title_original: Sharing is caring: Attestable and Trusted Workflows out of Distrustful Components
e04973bf5f0ed53bf288ff40.excerpt: arXiv:2603.03403v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) protect private memory and attest initial code and configuration, but neither constrain nor attest shared channels between TEEs or with the untrusted host. Confidentiality thus depends on the functional correctness of all in-TEE code accessing these channels: a single misuse can leak data and compromise a pipeline. This assumption is increasingly untenable for agentic applications that generate code at runtime and cloud pipelines of mutually distrustful components. We present MICA, a confidential-computing firmware extension that decouples confidentiality from trust in in-TEE code. MICA lets tenants define, restrict, and attest channel constraints between TEEs and with the untrusted host, including transitive constraints spanning a pipeline. It extends attestation to groups of communicating TEEs, letting external parties verify the confidentiality properties induced by these constraints across a pipeline. We implement MICA on Arm CCA by extending the Realm Management Monitor with a small policy language, requiring no hardware changes and minor QEMU and KVM changes. Our evaluation demonstrates support for confidential agentic applications and pipeline computations without trusting the functional correctness of in-TEE code. MICA increases the TCB by 7% and incurs infrequent setup costs: 2-4% boot-time overhead, approximately 1.5 s for policy upload, and 246-598 ms for group attestation. On

a41638cb7e32b5049dafe2f9.title_original: The Infinite Mutation Engine? Measuring Polymorphism in LLM-Generated Offensive Code
a41638cb7e32b5049dafe2f9.excerpt: arXiv:2605.03619v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Malware authors traditionally rely on polymorphic techniques to produce variants within a malware family, complicating detection. Generative AI enables attackers to automatically synthesize structurally diverse payloads with identical behavior, raising the question of how much evasion Large Language Models (LLMs) actually provide. Recent work has assumed that LLMs can produce highly polymorphic payloads, leaving unquantified the variation that emerges when an attacker repeatedly generates a payload, or explicitly instructs the model to avoid prior implementations. In this work, we address this gap by measuring the polymorphic capacity of a commercial model (Claude Opus~4.6) acting as an automated malware generator. We build a dual-agent, four-stage pipeline that generates, tests, and refines a data-exfiltration payload comprising file traversal, encryption, exfiltration, and integration. We produce payloads under two settings: (a) functional prompting, and (b) explicit prompting injecting a structured history of prior variants. Evaluating structural (TEDs) and semantic (embeddings) variance, we find that explicit prompting fragments the structural space, creating variants that are hard to cluster for some ML classifiers. This structural diversity is operationally cheap, costing \$0.41--\$0.73 per validated payload. However, static n-gram analysis reveals that because the LLM treats inter-module boundaries as immutable, a sin

5692a0f32d3f0bb6f677e914.title_original: SciIntBench: Measuring LLM Compliance with Research Integrity Norms Under Adversarial Framing
5692a0f32d3f0bb6f677e914.excerpt: arXiv:2605.29468v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support scientific work, but it is unclear whether they uphold responsible conduct of research (RCR) norms or help undermine them. We introduce SciIntBench, an adversarial benchmark of 1350 prompts across 270 scenarios, ten RCR categories, and three scientific domains. Each scenario appears in five gradations, from Most Overt to Most Covert adversarial prompts, and an additional Benign version, allowing us to jointly measure framing-sensitive refusal of misconduct and helpfulness on legitimate requests. We evaluate 16 commercial and open-weight LLMs from six providers (2024--2026), producing 21,600 responses. We assess the responses using LLM judgments validated by human evaluation, achieving high agreement ($\kappa$ = 0.857). We find that, under the most covert framing condition, models fail to refuse requests for research misconduct in 71.7\% of cases, on average. Refusals vary by RCR category, with weaker boundaries around transparency, plagiarism, and fabrication.

b7072a0b2a4e4f7eecb1f174.title_original: Evidence-Bound Gateway-Path Provenance for Third-Party LLM Inference
b7072a0b2a4e4f7eecb1f174.excerpt: arXiv:2606.22560v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Third-party LLM gateways select providers, models, endpoints, and fallback paths while also authoring the records used to explain and bill those decisions. We present evidence-bound gateway-path provenance, which makes these decisions subject to client-verifiable request contracts. An attested mediation runtime intersects a signed service policy with the client's authorization, constructs provider-facing calls, and protects streamed responses. The contract distinguishes initial routes from fallback destinations and admits each transition only after an authorized failure. A signed close-out binds the execution trace, provider-reported usage, authorized pricing, and complete response. We formalize the protocol state machine and establish authorization preservation, execution and stream binding, charge integrity, and channel confidentiality relative to the public receipt metadata. The analysis also characterizes replay, runtime replacement, and the information disclosed by public payload commitments. Controlled software-path measurements show 0.442 ms paired p95 latency overhead at concurrency one, peak throughput of 10.65 thousand requests/s, and stream close-out below 0.4 ms p95. An AWS Nitro Enclaves prototype completed 30 live single-route streaming requests with attestation-bound session and signing keys. The design separates gateway administration from payload processing and supplies a verifiable account of each confirmed

28054c3550bc966f52237174.title_original: Auditable and Transparent Fully Authenticated Disk Encryption via USB Storage Interposition
28054c3550bc966f52237174.excerpt: arXiv:2607.12716v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Full Disk Encryption (FDE) has become increasingly important in the last decades due to the evident confidentiality concerns. In most systems, encryption is provided by an operating system driver, through which the user can transparently access the encrypted disk after supplying the required keys (or the credentials from which those keys are derived). In this work, we explore an alternative approach: the use of an intermediate USB device placed between the host system and the external hard disk, where the encrypted data are stored. Although there are existing devices that follow this inline approach (such as RAID controllers and USB enclosures with built-in encryption), we explore the use of a general-purpose single-board computer running Linux with USB On-The-Go support (e.g. a Raspberry Pi), to provide FADE (Fully Authenticated Disk Encryption). Our system, named CC (Cryptographic Companion), performs the cryptographic operations (encryption/decryption and authentication), providing a standard USB mass-storage interface to the host (which is entirely unaware of the presence of encryption) while relying on the external USB hard disk to store the corresponding encrypted blocks. Our design provides several key advantages: flexibility, low cost, transparency, the use of generic hardware and free and open-source software, adaptability to emerging cryptographic schemes, and mitigations against malicious disk firmware. This paper

213cb4310fa9d0d52eeeaa2b.title_original: How Agents Ask for Permission: User Permissions for AI Agents, from Interfaces to Enforcement
213cb4310fa9d0d52eeeaa2b.excerpt: arXiv:2607.13718v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As AI agents grow in prevalence, so too do their risks to users, creating a need for robust and usable systems for agent permissions. Many recent proposals implement product-level permissions, where the same security policy is applied for all users of a given agent framework. Yet different users have varying needs, necessitating support for user-level permission policies in agentic AI systems. We survey 21 proposed user-level agent permissions systems and construct a taxonomy of approaches to specifying, deriving, and enforcing user-level permissions. We further analyze and compare against five commercial agents. We find that despite a wide diversity of proposals, sizable gaps remain in usability, transparency, and user control, particularly between academic and commercial agents.

b11e23d03fefec3a0a784753.title_original: Every Model Cheats: Prompt-Level Mitigation of Cheating on Offensive Cyber Tasks
b11e23d03fefec3a0a784753.excerpt: arXiv:2607.21763v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely cheat on cybersecurity benchmarks, inflating reported pass rates far beyond genuine capability. Prior audits of Cybench found cheating in 0.3-3.4% of traces, implicating only a handful of models. We present a controlled prompt-ablation study across 22 frontier models from 7 providers on 23 Cybench capture-the-flag (CTF) challenges under three prompt conditions (no anti-cheat, standard, severe). All 1,518 task traces were individually audited through a four-stage pipeline combining LLM-as-a-judge classification, programmatic verification, judge-verifier reconciliation, and human review. We find cheating is far more pervasive than previously estimated: under baseline conditions, 37.1% of passes involved cheating, 21 of 22 models cheated, and scores were inflated by up to 5x. Anti-cheat prompts reduce cheat propensity from 33.0% (baseline) to 18.6% (standard) to 8.5% (severe) without degrading, and sometimes improving, solve rates. However, even under the most restrictive prompt condition, eight models still produced cheated passes, and cheating shifted from web search toward infrastructure probing. We introduce the "solve rate" metric (clean passes only) to distinguish genuine capability from cheated outcomes, and argue it should be standard practice in any evaluation where cheating vectors are available. Anti-cheat prompts are an effective and essentially free first layer of mitigat

893b5d727bfd443177bdc79f.title_original: An AI Approach to Verified Production Cryptographic Libraries
893b5d727bfd443177bdc79f.excerpt: arXiv:2608.00965v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cryptographic code is critical infrastructure that must be correct, yet formally verifying production libraries remains difficult. Existing language-model proof systems solve isolated obligations with specifications and premises already given, leaving production-library verification unresolved. We present CryptoProver, an AI-based system that synthesizes internal specifications and Verus-checked proofs from high-level API contracts. Without changing executable code, CryptoProver constructs a new independent proof of curve25519-dalek and verifies RustCrypto's previously unverified chacha20 implementation against an RFC 8439 specification. These cryptographic lineages underpin deployed systems including Signal and Shadowsocks; Signal has an estimated 218M global downloads. The original developers report a focused five-month, three-person effort to verify curve25519-dalek. Given the API contracts and a fixed trusted library of field specifications, arithmetic facts, axioms, and vstd, CryptoProver synthesizes the internal specifications and proofs in 11.4 hours with USD 466.99 in recorded API cost. CryptoProver follows a trust-first design principle: mechanical gates reject specification weakening, invented axioms, and cross-module breakage, while isolation blocks reference proof retrieval, including from git history.

a6570c12f81f5a7c37fab023.title_original: Agenra: A Language and Verified Core for Stateful LLM Agent Authorization
a6570c12f81f5a7c37fab023.excerpt: arXiv:2608.22868v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Applications that deploy LLM agents keep revising the permissions their agents use. When authority is consumable, even widening a permission can break a legitimate workflow, because an early call may use up a grant that a later call needs. Checking individual requests, or watching one run succeed, misses this. We present Agenra, a policy language with a Lean enforcement core that tracks the values each call uses, resources discovered at run time, and authority consumed by earlier calls. Agenra treats safety and workflow preservation as separate properties. Our key idea is to certify a revision with a simulation between the old and new permission ledgers. Quota increases, appended grants and independent reorderings admit such simulations by construction, and Lean checks proposed simulations for other finite-quota revisions. The proofs use the deployed matching predicates and extend through the full monitor, covering discovered resources, payloads that are never enumerated, failed calls and approvals. They assume serialized calls and identical service results under both policies, and they trust the Python translation layer. On 51 authored revisions, the checks certify all 21 that preserve their clients and none of the 30 that do not, and every lost workflow is confirmed by replay. They also certify a real quota increase from an open-source agent application. In a report-delivery application, raising the send quota preserves ev

8e53f721a176dcfcbdadb19a.title_original: Capability-Gated Language Models: Security Composes, Utility Does Not
8e53f721a176dcfcbdadb19a.excerpt: arXiv:2609.00445v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deployed language model safeguards (safety fine-tuning, filtering, unlearning) vary by principal only outside the model weights: filters are reconfigured, tiers are multiplied, and artefacts are reissued; inside one set of weights every request meets the same model configuration. This motivates us to define capability-gated deployment: per-principal access control inside one set of weights, whose configurations form a lattice - meets accumulate a principal's restrictions and joins pool a coalition's reach. We instantiate it by sparse rank gating over an existing nested-factorisation mechanism, guide profile search with one-pass attribution, and read every result once from a pre-registered held-out split. Security approximately composes: provably exactly at meets under a monotone-elicitation assumption we falsify pointwise. In two lineages the median held-out meet deepens suppression; the one effect surviving correction strengthens it. Utility does not: individually harmless profiles can compose to retention and fluency damage, and no compositional bound exists.

a46b06e6f8fe444c1d6e35b7.title_original: Actions with Receipts: Jointly Binding Claims, Evidence, and Execution for Replayable Tool-Agent Auditing
a46b06e6f8fe444c1d6e35b7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.00327v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tool-using agents can expose citations and execution logs while leaving a critical association unaudited: whether the claim shown to a user is the claim emitted by the committed execution and supported by the cited source. A valid citation and a valid trace can therefore remain individually well formed while being transplanted across claims, actions, runs, or source versions. We introduce a claim-anchored execution contract that jointly binds the emitted claim, its exact source span, the ordered execution prefix that produced it, and the source version and access state observed by that execution. Each receipt contains an emission anchor that deterministically locates the claim inside a committed answer or claim-bearing action, together with source identifiers, offsets, hashes, quotes, and a domain-separated execution commitment. A deterministic integrity verifier reconstructs these bindings before semantic or task labels are joined. We separate this integrity plane from a pluggable support plane, so structural validity is not used as a proxy for entailment. The contract exposes seven independently testable properties: claim-emission binding, source binding, ordered-execution binding, oracle separation, persisted-object replay, execution-rerun consistency, and version/access binding. Across 1,280 cross-object attacks, the joint contract detects 1,275 substitutions (0.9961). Removing a targeted property reduces its attack-dete

156c37dcde449d4ad6816b5b.title_original: CHAMP: Cayley HAshing with Matrix Products
156c37dcde449d4ad6816b5b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.04442v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cayley hash functions hash binary strings by representing the bits of the message as elements of a semigroup and multiplying the corresponding elements. This gives Cayley hash functions useful homomorphic properties. Here, we propose CHAMP, a Cayley hash function based on products of 2 by 2 matrices over a finite field, and discuss its security, implementation, and performance.

c51ee187f2e62c2a9eb8a055.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16550v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: General-purpose frontier models are large, expensive to run, and increasingly reluctant to engage with authorised defensive- and offensive-security work. We ask the opposite question: how small can a cybersecurity-specialist transformer be while remaining genuinely useful to a security practitioner? We introduce CT0, a Cybersecurity Transformer architecture, and CT0-Micro, its first incarnation: a compact (~4B-parameter) model built on the open base model, whose backbone is specialised by two-phase on-policy distillation on our Cybersecurity AI (CAI) dataset. CT0 serves two modes from one set of weights: System 1 answers typed security decisions (is this file suspicious, is this request an attack, did the model just refuse) in a single forward pass without generating a token, System 2 is the usual tool-using agent, and a confidence gate spends generation only where the fast path is unsure. Specialisation lifts the agentic path: CT0-Micro solves 21.1% of cybench-subtask against 7.6% for its base, above every open model of comparable footprint and the densest cybersecurity capability per parameter we measured. The fast path is what the architecture buys: CT0-Micro screens eighty files per second for indicators of compromise, catches its own refusals at 96.5% accuracy in 47 ms where the model judging itself reaches 76.5% in 254 ms and misses half of them, flags jailbreak requests at AUROC 0.966 in 8 ms, and, generating only for

bf5039b04b4f9b3b8c29f144.title_original: Harnessing Trust in Directed Graphs: Redefining Robustness of Graph Learning
bf5039b04b4f9b3b8c29f144.excerpt: arXiv:2306.02002v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Existing research on robust Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) focuses predominantly on undirected graphs, overlooking the trustworthiness inherent in the link directions of directed graphs. In this work, we analyze the limitations of current approaches from both the attack and defense perspectives and redefine the robustness of GNNs in directed graphs. From the attack side, we introduce a more realistic directed graph attack setting that addresses the shortcomings of existing attacks. From the defense side, we propose a simple yet effective message-passing framework that serves as a plug-in layer to strengthen GNN robustness while avoiding a false sense of robustness. Our findings show that the trust signals encoded in directed graphs can be harnessed to substantially improve the robustness of GNNs. When combined with existing defense strategies, the framework achieves state-of-the-art robust performance alongside strong clean accuracy against both transfer and adaptive attacks. These results point to a novel and promising direction for strengthening the robustness of graph deep learning.

9000b4327567aea846fad6e8.title_original: A Deeper Dive into the Irreversibility of PolyProtect: Making Protected Face Templates Harder to Invert
9000b4327567aea846fad6e8.excerpt: arXiv:2605.03857v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work presents a deeper analysis of the "irreversibility" property of PolyProtect, a biometric template protection method initially proposed for securing face embeddings. PolyProtect transforms embeddings into protected templates via multivariate polynomials, whose coefficients and exponents are distinct for each subject enrolled in the face recognition system. A polynomial is applied to consecutive sets of elements from a given embedding, where the amount of overlap between the sets is a tunable parameter. We begin our irreversibility analysis by demonstrating that PolyProtected templates are easier to invert using a numerical solver based on cosine distance, as opposed to Euclidean distance (used in the earlier PolyProtect work). To make this inversion more difficult, we then propose a "key selection algorithm", which tries to choose "keys" (coefficients and exponents of the PolyProtect polynomial) that enhance the irreversibility of PolyProtected templates, compared to when the keys are purely random. Our experiments show that this algorithm is effective at generating PolyProtected templates that are significantly more difficult to invert, and that it approximately equalises the irreversibility of PolyProtected templates generated using different "overlap" parameters. This allows for better control of the known irreversibility versus accuracy trade-off across different overlaps. We also show that accuracy in the

e263be56685d0755ce6dfcb6.title_original: Exponentially Fewer-Server PIR from Sparser $S$-Decoding Polynomials
e263be56685d0755ce6dfcb6.excerpt: arXiv:2607.22033v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that under a plausible number-theoretic conjecture, for any constant $s$ there exists an $s$-server private information retrieval (PIR) protocol that on an $n$-bit database requires communication $\exp(O((\log n)^{1/s} (\log \log n)^{1-1/s}))$. This achieves a superpolynomial improvement in communication when $s \geq 4$; previous constructions attaining the same communication required $2^{O(s)}$ servers. Our number-theoretic conjecture is implied by existing conjectures, namely the generalized repunit conjecture and Schinzel's hypothesis H (either one of these conjectures would suffice alone). Our result builds on the "matching vector family + $S$-decoding polynomials" framework pioneered by Efremenko (STOC 2009) and recently refined by Ghasemi, Kopparty, and Sudan (STOC 2025). The main ingredient is a framework for constructing $S$-decoding polynomials with only $k+1$ nonzero coefficients modulo special products of $k$ primes, resolving an open problem posed by Ghasemi and Kopparty (ITCS 2026). By the lower bound shown by Ghasemi and Kopparty, this is the minimum achievable sparsity. We also empirically validate our construction and make our result unconditional for all $s \leq 15$. We also apply our techniques to regimes where $s$ grows with $n$, showing under a stronger variant of our number-theoretic conjecture that the communication complexity of $s$-server matching-vector PIR can be superpolynomially redu

3c1d8fa65af6232bba2dc48c.title_original: VStress: Correlation-Aware Auditing and Adaptive Budget Allocation for Repeated Verifiers
3c1d8fa65af6232bba2dc48c.excerpt: arXiv:2609.36958v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Repeated verifier calls are useful only when they contribute conditional information. We introduce VStress, an auditable replay contract, and VStress-CA, a correlation-aware allocation policy that estimates the conditional marginal information of an unqueried verifier on a sealed calibration split, discounts uncertainty, normalizes by call cost, and stops or abstains when the next call is not informative. The controller freezes its decision and cost ledger before joining the clean oracle; a dependence-shift alarm disables channel preference and falls back to exact-stop. The controlled audit gives the mechanism boundary: at 35% symmetric corruption, majority-5 improves balanced accuracy from 0.6578 to 0.7739, whereas at 65% it loses 0.1226 points. In the matched fixed-budget comparison, breadth, redundancy, and adaptive allocation obtain balanced accuracies 0.6048, 0.6375, and 0.6538, with 3.4216 calls per item and an RLVR score of 0.6417 for VStress-CA. Dependence diagnostics also increase from same-model repeats to cross-family channels, with conditional marginal gains of 0.0126, 0.0462, and 0.0913. These measurements turn correlation from a post-hoc warning into an auditable allocation decision.

2d2580e2939e47617a992636.title_original: Rethinking Quality in Large Language Model Routing: Security-Conditioned Model-and-Budget Selection
2d2580e2939e47617a992636.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18566v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) routers reduce serving cost by choosing which model to call and how many output tokens to grant it for each query. Existing routers rank model-budget actions using a single quality metric. This does not work for mixed workloads. For ordinary queries, a good answer is correct and useful (utility); for security-sensitive queries, a good answer refuses harmful requests or resists malicious instructions (security). These two objectives prefer different models and budgets. We propose SCRouter, a router that learns when to prioritize security and how to allocate the token budget. For each model-budget pair, it estimates the probability that the response finishes within budget. It uses this probability to predict utility and security separately. A small probe determines how to weight these two predictions for each query. SCRouter then selects the model and budget by balancing the weighted utility and security against cost. We also build SCRouterBench, a benchmark of 38,869 utility and security queries spanning nine security dimensions, each answered under all 144 combinations of 12 models and 12 budgets, plus 2,753 out-of-domain queries. SCRouter improves the baselines by 13-29 points in-domain and 19-23 points out-of-domain.

CVE-2026-110024.description: @fastify/jwt is a JWT utility plugin for Fastify. In versions prior to 10.2.5, the top-level sign and verify methods replace the globally configured defaults with the per-call options instead of merging them, so passing any per-call option silently drops every global default that the call does not restate, including temporal protections such as token expiration and maximum accepted token age. A token signed this way carries no expiration claim and never expires, and verification stops enforcing a configured maximum age, so stale or never-expiring tokens are accepted. The route-level decorators for signing and verifying already merge options and are not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/jwt 10.2.5, and users should upgrade to 10.2.5 or later.
CVE-2026-110024.summary_ko: @fastify/jwt에서 최상위 sign 및 verify 메서드가 전역 설정된 기본값을 병합하지 않고 호출별 옵션으로 대체합니다. 이로 인해 토큰 만료 등의 시간 기반 보호 기능이 누락될 수 있습니다.

Performing a manipulation results in cross-site request forgery. The attack may be initiated remotely. Upgrading to version 1.17.0-beta.1 can resolve this issue. The patch is named 39fbae87b38573616a1a3b152cdb292787bb1109. It is advisable to upgrade the affected component.
