e68890b14f274817eab389e7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.26642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit DM-RSA, an RSA variant that uses two independent moduli, whose original version was broken by H{\aa}stad's attack and contained an incorrect compromise-tolerance claim. We give a formal treatment of its repaired variant, DM-RSA-OAEP: (i) a complete IND-CCA2 security proof in the random-oracle model via a two-step hybrid argument, upper-bounding the security of the scheme by that of the weaker underlying RSA-OAEP instance, with an explicit simulation loss; (ii) a fault-detection theorem in an explicit adversary model that covers computation, key, and verification faults, including safe-error attacks, under a clearly stated physical-diversity assumption; (iii) an explicit analysis of why the countermeasure degrades to uselessness when the diversity assumption is violated (common-mode faults on a single chip). We position the scheme against the countermeasure landscape and against the broken dual-modulus literature. The contribution is deliberately framed as a fault countermeasure with a provable detection guarantee, not as a computationally stronger RSA. We conclude with a concrete instantiation and a detailed measurement protocol.

892d5f5f2de13b8f9269d8ef.excerpt: arXiv:2610.26713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bitcoin-style Proof-of-Work (PoW) secures permissionless blockchains but spends substantial computation on hash puzzles which have no utility other than extending the chain. At the same time, we have seen that the rise of generative AI has created significant demand for computational resources that are unfortunately available only to a few players. We propose a solution that solves both problems at the same time. In particular, we present Proof-of-ML-Inference (PoML), a consensus protocol in which miners perform user-requested machine-learning inference as part of their consensus algorithm. We identify exactly what computational assumptions are needed for ML inference to safely replace hash work, formalize those assumptions, and give evidence that LLMs and diffusion models satisfy them. We then formally analyse the security of our protocol by reducing the security of our protocol to the security of the Bitcoin Backbone model. Finally, we empirically evaluate block-time stability, showing that, in a simulated environment, PoML maintains a block production rate close to its calibrated block-time target.

f14554685763767bf73f3913.title_original: Accountable partial understanding: securing the epistemic attack surface of agentic systems
f14554685763767bf73f3913.excerpt: arXiv:2610.26799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attackers profit from what defenders do not understand. Software security has treated the gap between system behavior and human comprehension as a condition to narrow through analysis and assurance, booking the remainder as accepted risk. Agentic AI systems change that gap: when software reads, writes, explains, and authorizes security-relevant behavior, partial understanding moves faster, grows more opaque, and couples to delegated authority. This paper characterizes the resulting epistemic attack surface and presents a taxonomy of four interacting attack categories, which target the interpretation of intent, the production and consumption of evidence, the scope of delegated authority, and the comprehension of human supervisors. It then defines accountable partial understanding (APU) and specifies six necessary conditions: bounded scope with explicit assumptions, inspectable evidence, assigned responsibility, visible residual unknowns, actionability, and temporal maintenance. It explains why delegating interpretation to software agents differs from distributing knowledge among people and distinguishes APU from risk acceptance, explainable AI, assurance cases, formal verification, and human-in-the-loop oversight. From the conditions, the paper derives five design principles: bounded delegation, decoupled evidence, assumption tracking with invalidation, role-specific accountability views, and intervention-preserving design with r

367bbfacfc2e71dd476506f9.title_original: Predicting CVSS and CWE from CVE Descriptions with Fine-Tuned Small Language Models
367bbfacfc2e71dd476506f9.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24297v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Until April 2026, the National Vulnerability Database labeled nearly every published Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry with a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v3.1 vector, a severity tier, and a Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) weakness type. Now, NIST enriches only the high priority CVEs, leaving many newly published vulnerabilities unlabelled with the classifiers that security teams use for patch triage. In CVE enrichment, we predict the eight base components of CVSS v3.1 vector, base score, severity tier, and CWE from the vulnerability's textual description alone. To prevent leakage between near-duplicate descriptions, all systems are trained only on CVEs published in 2022 and 2023. Results are evaluated on all 36,325 usable 2024 CVEs in the pinned NVD snapshot. All scores are either directly predicted, or calculated from predicted vectors using the CVSS formula. A fine-tuned 3.8B-parameter model Phi-3.5-mini, trained with LoRA in 2.5 hours on a single Apple M5 Pro chip, achieves 69.9% accuracy on severity and 70.9% on CWE. It matches the official vector exactly for 48.8% of test CVEs, outperforming TF-IDF logistic regression by 2.8 to 4.7 points on all accuracy metrics based on zero-exclusion paired bootstrap intervals. When we evaluate the base model with a zero-shot prompt, it achieves 20.8% accuracy on severity in a sample of 2,000 CVEs. In this same sample, its stated scores match its own vect

705577c2fe7c3e29b18dbf4d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24477v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study differentially private black-box evaluation of arbitrary high-dimensional functions. Given a dataset $S$ and query access to a function $f$---whose sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded---the goal is to privately output an approximation to $f(S)$. The black-box evaluator can only query the value of $f$ over a down neighborhood of $S$ (i.e., those subsets of $S$ that are obtained by removing a bounded number of elements from $S$). We design generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy through a reduction to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (QCO). Our black-box evaluator enjoys a geometric notion of utility. Consider the vectors obtained by applying $f$ on sets in a down neighborhood of $S$. With high probability, the evaluator's output is guaranteed to be in the convex hull of these vectors. Our work generalizes the result of Linder et al. [LRSS25] for real-valued function evaluation to high dimensions. It also recovers the private center-point guarantees of Beimel et al. [BMNS19], with an explicit additive approximation to maximum Tukey depth. We also apply our evaluators to user-level quasi-concave and convex optimization, showing how they can improve upon the sample-and-aggregate baseline of Nissim et al. [NRS07] by replacing the multiplicative data overhead with an additive overhead. Finally, we show that our formulation of high dimensional black-box evaluatio

6318e9d07abcc0231983f2fd.title_original: Effective Construction of Feature Database of Fingerprinting Functions for Code-Clone SCA
6318e9d07abcc0231983f2fd.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24479v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In contemporary software development, the extensive adoption of third-party libraries has become standard practice to avoid reinventing the wheel. This trend is particularly evident in programming ecosystems that lack mature package managers, such as C/C++. Within this context, Code Clone Detection (CCD) techniques have emerged as essential tools for identifying instances of code reuse, thereby mitigating security and legal concerns. Despite significant advances in CCD algorithms, a notable gap persists between academic tools and real-world applications. This disparity primarily arises because academic tools rely on experimental datasets composed of a limited number of indexed repositories, whereas real-world applications require a much broader scope of code sources. To address this challenge, we propose a novel, systematic approach for selecting appropriate open-source repositories to construct a more effective CCD feature dataset. Our method, OSSScope, employs a greedy algorithm to analyze the diversity of fingerprinting functions across 2.55 million C repositories on GitHub, maximizing unique fingerprinting functions while minimizing the number of repositories required. OSSScope compiles an optimal feature dataset containing 61 million fingerprinting functions from 190K repositories, resulting in a 22.65% improvement in recall over SOTA tools, and covers over 95% of the features from other sources. Leveraging the selected r

8b44b817a58acef827f217a8.title_original: Fast \(\ell_\infty\)-Reduction of Rank-2 Lattices in $\mathbb{R}^n$ via a New Reduced-Basis Notion
8b44b817a58acef827f217a8.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24719v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The shortest vector problem (SVP) under the infinity norm ($\ell_\infty$-norm) is an important lattice problem with applications in lattice-based cryptography. In particular, the security analysis of the post-quantum signature standard ML-DSA highlights the importance of finding short solutions satisfying infinity-norm constraints, rather than only Euclidean norm bounds. However, most existing lattice reduction algorithms are developed for the Euclidean norm, while dedicated studies under the infinity norm remain limited. In this work, we focus on rank-two lattices in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and introduce a new notion of reduced basis under the infinity norm. Based on this definition, we propose an efficient lattice basis reduction algorithm that performs a multi-dimensional analogue of Euclidean division using a dominant coordinate of the basis vectors. Each non-terminal iteration guarantees a factor-two decrease of the maximum infinity norm of the basis vectors. We prove that the algorithm terminates and achieves a bit complexity of $O(nT^2)$, matching the asymptotic complexity order of the classical Lagrange--Gauss reduction. Moreover, the proposed algorithm saves at least $2n$ multiplications per iteration compared with the classical approach. Experiments demonstrate significant runtime improvements, especially for high-dimensional lattices. This work provides a foundation for developing lattice reduction techniques under the infin

cd72678e9ccd76f1c33dbc35.title_original: Collaborative Hand Drawing to Conceptualize Usable Privacy and Security Research Problems: Students' Perspectives (Extended Version)
cd72678e9ccd76f1c33dbc35.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24748v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we explore students' perspectives on incorporating hand drawing to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems. We surveyed 64 female students who participated in an in-class collaborative hand drawing activity to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems as part of a group-based student research project on usable privacy and security in an information and computer security course for undergraduate students. Our survey responses suggest that students perceived the drawing exercise positively. That is, they found it helpful in several aspects, enjoyable, and they recommend it to other students taking the course. The students also said that they would like to have such an exercise in other courses, such as Principles of Human-Computer Interaction and Fundamentals of Data Networks. Only three students mentioned downsides of the exercise, namely doubts about their drawing skills. Our results provide useful insights for educators seeking to enhance the student learning experience.

2c8a706d986abb3d5c14e79f.title_original: BitPCE: Batched Multi-Dimensional PolicyResolution with GPU Bitmap Algebra
2c8a706d986abb3d5c14e79f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24974v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Policy controllers must determine which workloads match rules spanning several label dimensions. Hash sets, compressed bitmaps, and GPU set-processing primitives address the underlying set operations. However, intermediate results, repeated scope evaluations, dependent policy updates, and host transfers can dominate the cost of a heterogeneous batch. We study this problem as batched intersection-of-unions (IoU). Our design exploits independent scope--word tasks, reusable endpoint expressions, and policy dependencies. The challenges are preserving wildcard, empty-group, and exclusion semantics, recognizing equal scopes, and retaining unchanged recipients affected by source edits. BitPCE addresses them with register-resident GPU evaluation, canonical scope compilation, and dependency-complete candidate selection under a stated rendering contract. IP-only changes reuse cached memberships. We establish correctness and word-work bounds. On a four-vCPU A10G host, resident GPU execution is 3.46--36.60$\times$ faster than the best tested native CPU path, including CRoaring, and 1.14--2.22$\times$ faster than an adapted operand-parallel GPU reduction. Gains narrow at the host-output boundary: on an eight-vCPU host, including upload and compact identifier output, resolution takes 16.3 ms versus 19.3 ms for CPU at 100K objects and 500 scopes. Sparse labels and small batches can favor CPU execution. Scope reuse, candidate selection, and i

2d0d3eed5f4521a98334c2e7.title_original: Hierarchical Rule Auditing with Exact Ternary GPU Correlation
2d0d3eed5f4521a98334c2e7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24997v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Auditing firewall logs against requirements mapped to controls and frameworks must retain overlapping obligations, preserve uncertainty from missing attributes and count distinct affected records. Direct, bitmap and relational methods can express this audit; a correlation implementation must preserve distinctions that ordinary match counts and rule-hit totals discard. We present an exact ternary correlation algorithm that compiles categorical conjunctions into one bounded-integer matrix product. A dominating false-predicate penalty separates known mismatches from missing evidence, while per-record hierarchy unions prevent duplicate counting. We prove their composition and handle high-cardinality endpoints through exact address classes and versioned labels. Evaluation compares eight CPU/GPU implementations, includes public traffic and 133 published source-address ACLs with generated observations, and measures hierarchy and policy-rebuild costs. On an NVIDIA L4, matched fused execution reduces latency by 8.8 to 11.2 percent relative to two-product correlation across five tested shapes. At 100,000 records and 1,024 requirements, it takes 12.28 ms versus 13.82 ms for two products and 12.29 ms for GPU bitmaps. Bitmaps remain faster in most regimes, with hierarchy operations and reductions dominating the measured fused-correlation stage intervals.

ce140f0b2f4b39b781ff2da7.title_original: Fundamental Limits of Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation with User Dropouts in Federated Learning
ce140f0b2f4b39b781ff2da7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.25743v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of users' gradients or model updates without revealing individual values. With user dropouts, correlated random keys protect local gradients while allowing recovery of the desired gradient sum. We consider three phases: key distribution, masked-gradient upload, and mask elimination. Users establish correlated keys, upload masked gradients, and provide additional messages to eliminate residual aggregate masks. Existing information-theoretic schemes typically design mask-elimination communication for a prescribed dropout threshold and evaluate its cost under worst-case dropouts across the masked-gradient upload and mask-elimination phases. Such designs cannot adjust communication to actual dropout scenarios. Moreover, the randomness and communication costs of establishing correlated keys remain largely unexplored. To address these limitations, we formulate an adaptive secure aggregation framework under the T-colluding security constraint and construct a single scheme that supports all feasible dropout scenarios by adapting its communication to the actual number of dropouts. We establish converse bounds on four resources: key randomness, key-distribution communication, masked-gradient communication, and mask-elimination communication. The latter two bounds are characterized for each realized dropout set in the masked-gradient upload phase. The proposed scheme achieves the opt

003f517fbbc783f84c04954a.title_original: When Care Expands and Control Declines: Understanding Digital Privacy in End-of-Life Care
003f517fbbc783f84c04954a.excerpt: arXiv:2610.25773v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Terminally ill patients generate extensive digital health data through hospital portals, physiological monitoring devices, consumer health applications, and end-of-life care platforms. Yet their ability to control this data is systematically undermined by the structural conditions of terminal care. Through semi-structured in-depth interviews with 21 terminally ill patients, 11 family caregivers, and 8 physicians recruited from tertiary hospitals, this study examines the digital privacy circumstances and subjective attitudes of patients in end-of-life contexts. Thematic analysis reveals five structural dimensions of digital privacy challenge: continuous bodily digitization without meaningful informed consent; cognitive decline driving involuntary proxy control of accounts; inferential data generation exceeding patients' epistemic boundaries; dissolution of individual privacy boundaries amid relational network restructuring; and the absence of institutional governance over post-mortem data. Patient privacy attitudes span three profiles: fundamental absence of privacy awareness, sustained active management under severe tool constraints, and perception of problems followed by resigned abandonment. Interviews with caregivers and physicians reveal benevolent substitution in the name of care needs, expansion of access beyond the initial task, and unresolved boundaries under absent institutional guidance. These findings reveal a compo

76b97e2f5e9aa72b4c1f341c.title_original: Blame-aware Recomposition for Secure Compilation Proofs of Low-Level Compartment Isolation
76b97e2f5e9aa72b4c1f341c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.26054v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The security guarantees of existing formally verified compilers for compartmentalized programs in unsafe languages like C stop at a rather high level, assuming a built-in protection mechanism and a block-based memory model. Verifying a concrete, low-level enforcement mechanism for compartment isolation is still a major challenge for current proof techniques. In particular, Abate et al.'s proof technique fails because one of their proof steps, recomposition, essentially requires hiding all information about the code of each compartment, which is not practically achievable at a low level. We propose an extension of their proof technique to a low-level setting where compartments can fully observe each other's code. To do so, we introduce an overlay semantics that allows us to characterize these observations as a form of undefined behaviour, and we use a novel variant of recomposition that we call blame-aware recomposition, which essentially allows recomposing executions as needed in the original high-level proof technique, even if the low-level context observes the code, because this context is ultimately going to be discarded. We apply this new proof to a compartment isolation mechanism that uses a programmable tag-based reference monitor.

fa3e55f772f4c51652b3aab0.title_original: BrushOff: Stroke-Based Re-rendering as a Watermark Removal Attack on Painting
fa3e55f772f4c51652b3aab0.excerpt: arXiv:2610.26682v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Invisible watermarks are used to mark who owns a painting. We show that a simple attack removes the most robust one we test. The attack redraws the watermarked painting with brush strokes, using a pretrained stroke-based renderer. We call this attack BrushOff. It needs no training, no knowledge of the watermark, and no generative model. We test four watermarks on 500 paintings from five styles. VINE, a recent watermark built to survive image editing, survives all 14 conventional distortions we test, with at least 97.8% detection. Repainting lowers its detection to 1.8%, while the output keeps a no-reference quality score close to that of the clean paintings. Diffusion regeneration can also remove VINE, but at the same removal level it moves the image twice as far from the painting in DreamSim distance, and it changes what the painting shows. Because the renderer draws a countable number of strokes, we can control the attack strength step by step. Finally, we test what kind of signal survives. A simple probe that stores bits in the relative brightness of neighboring regions survives repainting, while a probe that uses absolute brightness does not. The same probe fails under diffusion regeneration, while VINE fails under repainting. Robustness to these two attacks is therefore a separate property, and benchmarks should test both.

01670da5b5319fceb45670c1.title_original: Revisiting Shared Data Protection Against Key Exposure
01670da5b5319fceb45670c1.excerpt: arXiv:1901.08083v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper puts a new light on secure data storage inside distributed systems. Specifically, it revisits computational secret sharing in a situation where the encryption key is exposed to an attacker. It comes with several contributions: First, it defines a security model for encryption schemes, where we ask for additional resilience against exposure of the encryption key. Precisely we ask for (1) indistinguishability of plaintexts under full ciphertext knowledge, (2) indistinguishability for an adversary who learns: the encryption key, plus all but one share of the ciphertext. (2) relaxes the "all-or-nothing" property to a more realistic setting, where the ciphertext is transformed into a number of shares, such that the adversary can't access one of them. (1) asks that, unless the user's key is disclosed, noone else than the user can retrieve information about the plaintext. Second, it introduces a new computationally secure encryption-then-sharing scheme, that protects the data in the previously defined attacker model. It consists in data encryption followed by a linear transformation of the ciphertext, then its fragmentation into shares, along with secret sharing of the randomness used for encryption. The computational overhead in addition to data encryption is reduced by half with respect to state of the art. Third, it provides for the first time cryptographic proofs in this context of key exposure. It emphasizes that th

0a0dc6c4913a4f0298c8b1bc.title_original: Privacy-preserving Machine Learning in Internet of Vehicle Applications: Fundamentals, Recent Advances, and Future Direction
0a0dc6c4913a4f0298c8b1bc.excerpt: arXiv:2503.01089v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning (ML) in Internet of Vehicles (IoV) applications enhanced intelligent transportation, autonomous driving capabilities, and various connected services within a large, heterogeneous network. However, the increased connectivity and massive data exchange for ML applications introduce significant privacy challenges. Privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) offers potential solutions to address these challenges by preserving privacy at various stages of the ML pipeline. Despite the rapid development of ML-based IoV applications and the growing data privacy concerns, there are limited comprehensive studies on the adoption of PPML within this domain. Therefore, this study provides a comprehensive review of the fundamentals, recent advancements, and the challenges of integrating PPML into IoV applications. We first review existing surveys of various PPML techniques and their integration into IoV across different scopes. We then categorize IoV applications into three key domains and analyze the privacy challenges in leveraging ML in these application domains. Building on these fundamentals, we review recent advancements in integrating various PPML techniques within IoV applications, discussing their frameworks, key features, and performance in terms of privacy, utility, and efficiency. Finally, we identify current challenges and propose future research directions to enhance privacy and reliability in IoV applications

8fc21d3abaf9c7066fca25c0.title_original: Backdoor Attacks on Discrete Graph Diffusion Models
8fc21d3abaf9c7066fca25c0.excerpt: arXiv:2503.06340v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable generative capabilities in continuous data domains such as images and videos. Recently, discrete graph diffusion models (DGDMs) have extended this success to graph generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance. However, deploying DGDMs in safety-critical applications, such as drug discovery, poses significant risks without a thorough understanding of their security vulnerabilities. In this work, we conduct the first study of backdoor attacks on DGDMs, a potent threat that manipulates both the training and generation phases of graph diffusion. We begin by formalizing the threat model and then design a backdoor attack that enables the compromised model to: 1) generate high-quality, benign graphs when the backdoor is not activated, 2) produce effective, stealthy, and persistent backdoored graphs when triggered, and 3) preserve fundamental graph properties (permutation equivariance and exchangeability) even under attack. We validate 1) and 2) empirically, both with and without backdoor defenses, and support 3) through theoretical analysis inspired by prior work.

031fdad435f6125495d5ccb7.title_original: Redefining Hybrid Blockchains: A Balanced Architecture
031fdad435f6125495d5ccb7.excerpt: arXiv:2504.18966v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Blockchain technology has completely revolutionized the field of decentralized finance with the emergence of a variety of cryptocurrencies and digital assets. However, widespread adoption of this technology by governments and enterprises has been limited by concerns regarding the technology's scalability, governance, and economic sustainability. This paper aims to introduce a novel hybrid blockchain architecture that balances scalability, governance, and decentralization while being economically viable for all parties involved. The new semi-centralized model leverages strategies not prevalent in the field, such as resource and node isolation, containerization, separation of networking and compute layers, use of a Kafka pub-sub network instead of a peer-to-peer network, and stakes-based validator selection to possibly mitigate a variety of issues related to scalability, security, governance, and economic sustainability. Simulations conducted on Kubernetes demonstrate the architecture's ability to achieve over 1000 transactions per second, with consistent performance across scaled deployments, even on a lightweight consumer-grade laptop with resource constraints. The findings highlight the system's scalability, security, and economic viability, offering a robust framework for enterprise and government adoption.

95ebf0f09c4da41ce099b109.title_original: Cutting the Fuse: Actionable APT Attack Blocking in Provenance-based IDS
95ebf0f09c4da41ce099b109.excerpt: arXiv:2508.06073v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Provenance-based Intrusion Detection Systems (PIDS) are a critical line of defense against Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs). However, their practical deployment is crippled by alert flooding; state-of-the-art PIDS focus on detection performance, outputting thousands of low-information, unactionable alerts. These outputs fail to isolate the true cause of the detector's alert and cannot provide the security operations center(SOC) with actionable blocking strategies. To address this challenge, we propose ProvX, a novel APT defense framework designed for blocking attack steps within alerts. Unlike existing works, ProvX does not aim to merely improve attack detection performance; it is dedicated to transforming unactionable raw alerts into a core edge list for immediate review. Specifically, we introduce counterfactual explanation logic to reduce the alerts and find the minimal structural subset (i.e., the core attack edges) within an alert that determines its malicious prediction. This subset, when perturbed, can subvert the model's original prediction. The framework then applies a staged solidification strategy to enhance the precision and stability of the alert analysis. Ultimately, ProvX outputs an actionable core edge list for immediate response and blocking of critical attack steps. Experiments on DARPA datasets demonstrate that ProvX can locate key behaviors within alerts that are highly relevant to real-world attacks, a

76f839123303702be465b8da.title_original: Perspectives on Objectives and Design Principles in Offline Payments with Central Bank Digital Currency
76f839123303702be465b8da.excerpt: arXiv:2512.10636v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, fundamental design principles for a \textit{central bank digital currency} (CBDC) with offline functionality and corresponding countermeasures are discussed. We identify three major objectives relevant for core security and privacy properties of such CBDC proposals:(i) Access Control Security--- protection of a user's funds against unauthorized access by other users; (ii) Security against Depositor Misbehavior---preservation of the integrity of an environment (potentially the wallet) against misbehavior of its owner (for example, double-spending); (iii) Privacy by Design---ensuring privacy is embedded into the system architecture. Our central conclusion is based on the alignment of the objectives to concrete design elements as countermeasures; certain objectives and countermeasures have no or minimal interference with each other. A major consequence of our work is that the integrity of a user's wallet and, accordingly, the mitigation of double-spending race attacks should be addressed through the adaptation and integration of \textit{secure hardware} or functionally equivalent trusted execution mechanisms within a CBDC system. The developed framework is applied for the analysis of five academic proposals of payment systems.

2d85d05cd3132ee1d71bc66d.title_original: Authenticated Contradictions from Desynchronized Provenance and Watermarking
2d85d05cd3132ee1d71bc66d.excerpt: arXiv:2603.02378v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cryptographic provenance standards such as C2PA and invisible watermarking are positioned as complementary defenses for content authentication, yet the two verification layers are technically independent: neither conditions on the output of the other. This work formalizes and empirically demonstrates the $\textit{Integrity Clash}$, a condition in which a digital asset carries a cryptographically valid C2PA manifest asserting human authorship while its pixels simultaneously carry a watermark identifying it as AI-generated, with both signals passing their respective verification checks in isolation. We construct metadata washing workflows that produce these authenticated fakes through standard editing pipelines, requiring no cryptographic compromise, only the semantic omission of a single assertion field permitted by the current C2PA specification. To close this gap, we propose a cross-layer audit protocol that jointly evaluates provenance metadata and watermark detection status, achieving 100% classification accuracy across 3,500 test images spanning four conflict-matrix states and three realistic perturbation conditions. Our results demonstrate that the gap between these verification layers is unnecessary and technically straightforward to close.

95e55c86094adffb163fdc13.title_original: Estimating the Social Cost of Corporate Data Breaches
95e55c86094adffb163fdc13.excerpt: arXiv:2603.21270v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While the size of a data breach is typically measured by the number of (consumer, customer, or user) records exposed or compromised, its economic impact is generally measured from the point of view of the corporation suffering the data breach: cost in crisis management, legal fees, drop in stock price, and so on. This study examines whether it is possible to estimate the true cost, or the social cost of a data breach, measured by the impact on its victims and their out of pocket costs. To accomplish this we establish: (1) the estimation of the average direct financial losses of an identity theft (IDT) victim, including the opportunity cost of lost time, and healthcare expenditures associated with distress associated with identity theft; and (2) the estimation of increases in incidents of IDT that can be attributed to a major breach event. Our findings show that the average social cost per victim has declined significantly since 2016. Furthermore, we find that there is indeed a statistically significant increase in the number of IDTs following a mega-breach event when accounting for a discovery lag of 1-2 months post-breach. Applying our model to real-world cases allows us to estimate an upper and lower bound social cost of specific mega-breach events. We find that for the 2009 Heartland and 2013 Target breaches, even the conservative lower bound social cost estimate exceeded settlements by factors of 5 and 16, respectively.

4c354d794e93ff81f4afed18.title_original: DECKER: Domain-invariant Embedding for Cross-Keyboard Extraction and Recognition
4c354d794e93ff81f4afed18.excerpt: arXiv:2605.03384v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Acoustic side-channel attacks (ASCA) on keyboards pose a significant security risk, as keystrokes can be inferred from typing acoustics, revealing sensitive information. Prior ASCA studies are limited by small-scale datasets with restricted diversity in users, keyboards, and environments, constraining analysis across devices, microphones, and noise conditions. We introduce HEAR, a dataset designed to study ASCA along three axes: keyboard generalization, noise adaptation, and user bias. HEAR contains recordings from 53 participants using 37 laptop keyboards, collected in three realistic settings: (1) external microphone capture, (2) device microphone capture without network noise, and (3) VoIP-based streaming capture. This enables controlled evaluation across users, keyboards, and environments. On HEAR, we establish an ASCA benchmark spanning conventional features and pre-trained representations from raw audio and spectrograms in unimodal and multimodal settings. We propose DECKER, a domain-invariant keystroke inference framework with four stages: (1) Keyboard Signature Normalization to reduce device coloration, (2) domain-adversarial disentanglement to suppress keyboard identity, (3) supervised cross-keyboard contrastive alignment to enforce key consistency, and (4) Acoustic Style Randomization to synthesize unseen keyboard responses. We further explore sentence-level inference using an LLM-based post-processing layer to ref

b5dc35eb5208955419bc29eb.title_original: Devilray: A Reconfigurable Adversarial Baseline for Revealing Blind Spots in Fake Base Station Detection
b5dc35eb5208955419bc29eb.excerpt: arXiv:2605.19232v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fake Base Station (FBS) detection has been a critical focus of cellular security research for over two decades. However, significant financial and regulatory barriers to accessing commercial FBS (C-FBS) devices have limited direct visibility into real-world operations, forcing detection systems to be designed and evaluated around self-built prototypes. In this paper, we present Devilray, a reconfigurable adversarial baseline to guide effective FBS detection by exploring the realistic adversarial space and identifying blind spots in detection systems -- regions of realistic adversarial behavior excluded by prevailing threat models. To this end, we establish an empirical anchor through the first academic analysis of a C-FBS, define a fundamental four-phase pipeline and seven operational feature dimensions for adversarial behaviors, and extend them with operational variants derived from 3GPP standards analysis. Through combinatorial configurations of operations from commercial practices and specifications, Devilray enables the exploration of 2,592 FBS instances, spanning diverse operational possibilities. Using Devilray, we evaluate seven currently accessible FBS detectors and uncover coverage gaps across all seven, revealing blind spots rooted in assumption-bound design and evaluation. Our work provides an empirically grounded adversarial baseline for evaluating FBS detectors and guiding future detection design, with Devilray

e78644b7b81ab7b4b4bf0522.title_original: STRAL: What Adaptation Gains, Loses, and Costs in SOC Alert Screening
e78644b7b81ab7b4b4bf0522.excerpt: arXiv:2605.22324v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Security-alert screening must balance false-alert burden against missed important events, yet adaptation can change which events are detected. We investigate this trade-off using STRAL, a score-triggered active-learning controller combining ADWIN monitoring, selective label acquisition, and bounded model updates, with an optional historical validation Guard. Across four chronological alert-stream settings, we compare adaptive screening with a fixed, non-adapting baseline (Frozen), measuring recall, false-alert burden, detection preservation, and label-query costs. On two AMiner settings, STRAL reduces false positives by 21.4% (14 to 11) and 16.7% (6 to 5), respectively, while preserving all Frozen detections. On Wazuh, Guard reduces false positives by 9.8% (522 to 471), while losing two Frozen detections. On NAD-CD, STRAL raises recall from 36.11% to 40.29%, but loses 40.1% of Frozen detections while gaining 3,000 others; false positives increase by 151.2%. Guard preserves Frozen decisions on NAD-CD but requires 3,550 label queries, compared with 2,000 for STRAL. These findings demonstrate why adaptive SOC screening must be evaluated through detection preservation, false-alert burden, and feedback cost alongside aggregate recall.

9d318641e8f51772ae3000cb.excerpt: arXiv:2605.24941v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM agents increasingly combine long-term memory for personalization with tool calling for taking actions. We study a failure of this combination: personality-driven preferences stored in memory (e.g., cost-consciousness, impatience, risk tolerance) silently shifting tool-call parameters in contexts where they do not apply. We call this memory-induced tool-drift and stress-test it with MEMDRIFT, an iteratively refined benchmark of 105 scenarios spanning five bias dimensions and seven professional domains. Measured as excess parameter degradation over a neutral-memory baseline, biased memories in MEMDRIFT induce drift in all eight models we evaluate, raising degradation rates to 0.38--0.83 versus 0.05--0.12 for neutral memories. The drift persists under three widely used memory frameworks. A vulnerability audit of 6,062 tools across 288 MCP servers demonstrates that real-world tools are also susceptible to this failure mode. Mechanistically, we find that biased memories act as implicit steering vectors along the same direction as explicit behavioral instructions and draw attention away from task-relevant context. Neither prompt-based defenses nor relevance filters offer a complete solution, motivating defenses at the intersection of memory management and tool calling.

9305faf0dc343246455b5d5a.title_original: Semantic Validation of Packer Identification Tools: Characterization, Repair, and Downstream Impact
9305faf0dc343246455b5d5a.excerpt: arXiv:2605.25923v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Packer identification tools are essential to malware analysis, yet their semantic correctness remains largely unverified. Incorrect packer labels can trigger inappropriate unpacking and degrade downstream malware classification. This paper presents a framework for systematically exposing, characterizing, and repairing semantic errors in packer identification tools. Our key insight is to leverage unpackers as executable semantic contracts, enabling automated validation of packer predictions without requiring manually labeled packer ground truth. We develop a pipeline that normalizes heterogeneous tool outputs, localizes faulty decision logic, and repairs identification errors through complementary signatures, heuristic rules, and static unpacker-derived detection predicates. Our empirical evaluation reveals widespread identification failures, with an average packer family identification recall of only 44.8% and an average packedness detection recall of only 63.6%. The proposed two-stage repairs achieve an approximately 100.2% relative improvement in average packer family identification recall, while increasing packedness detection recall to 99.0%-99.5%. We further demonstrate that semantic errors can propagate through unpacking failures and adversely affect downstream malware classification. Correcting these errors improves average classification precision by 13.6 percentage points.

d61c66f7707027a124842e02.title_original: All-out Attack: Optimal Block Withholding Under Pay-Per-Share Scheme
d61c66f7707027a124842e02.excerpt: arXiv:2607.01209v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Classical Block Withholding (BWH) attacks have been extensively studied in block-dependent reward schemes, where pool members are compensated upon a block discovery within the pool. However, most contemporary mining pools operate under share-based schemes, wherein participants are paid immediately upon submission of valid shares. In this paper, we analyze BWH under Pay-Per-Share (PPS) for Nakamoto-style blockchains and prove that these mechanisms are not incentive compatible, contrary to conclusions drawn under fixed difficulty in prior literature. Under PPS, the optimal strategy for a BWH attacker is the All-out Attack (AoA): the adversary allocates its entire hashpower toward the victim pool, submitting only partial Proof-of-Work shares (pPoW) while withholding all valid blocks, i.e., full Proof-of-Work (fPoW). Prior to the first difficulty adjustment, the adversary incurs negligible loss from withheld fPoWs. After the adjustment reduces block difficulty, the adversary either generates more pPoWs per unit time when the pPoW difficulty is reduced accordingly or, if the pPoW difficulty is held fixed, earns a higher reward per share. In both cases, it achieves a post-adjustment reward rate of $\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}$ per target epoch, compared with the honest baseline rate of $\alpha$. Remarkably, this gain matches the theoretical upper bound achieved by optimal selfish mining in Nakamoto consensus under perfect network infl

955158207ca377fdff08dfb8.title_original: ShannonProver: Towards Automating Formal Cryptographic Proofs
955158207ca377fdff08dfb8.excerpt: arXiv:2607.02847v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cryptographic proofs are produced at a scale that increasingly exceeds the community's ability to verify them manually. Machine-checked proofs offer a path toward scalable proof verification, but they shift the bottleneck to writing the proofs themselves: even when the high-level proof plan is known, turning it into a proof script requires spelling out every detail the plan leaves implicit, which is laborious even for experts. This paper presents ShannonProver, an agentic system for automating cryptographic proofs. Given a protocol and its security definitions modeled by a cryptographer, ShannonProver decomposes the main theorem into intermediate games and lemmas, and constructs EasyCrypt proof scripts for those lemmas. We evaluate ShannonProver on a new dataset of lemmas in EasyCrypt. The benchmark spans textbook primitives, deployed standardized protocols, as well as recent NIST proposals, and includes expert case studies drawn from a corpus that has not previously been available online. On case studies such as ChaChaPoly1305 and MEE-CBC, ShannonProver completes within hours proof developments that historically took experts weeks to months. More broadly, this work suggests a path toward accelerating cryptographic research: as agents automate the proof-engineering burden, cryptographers can iterate more quickly on new constructions, obtain machine-checked assurance earlier, and bring protocols from design to deployment fast

981dec5381c6a71543a826e5.title_original: Flipping Minds by Flipping Bits: Decision-Level Cognitive Hijacking of Large Language Models
981dec5381c6a71543a826e5.excerpt: arXiv:2607.25227v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely applied in high-stakes decision-making scenarios such as corporate strategy, and users are increasingly relying on their outputs. However, the deep integration of open-source model sharing ecosystems with LLM-powered critical decision-making applications also introduces critical risks: if an attacker can manipulate the model's cognitive stance, they can indirectly influence the judgments and actions of downstream decision-makers. This paper defines such threats as decision-level hijacking. Existing attacks fail to achieve targeted cognitive manipulation without triggering prohibited content or degrading model functionality. To fill this gap, this paper reveals that Bit-Flip Attacks (BFAs) can serve as an attack vector for inducing decision-level hijacking, requiring no real-time interaction or control over the training process, and only a minimal number of weight bits need to be flipped after deployment to achieve stealthy, low-cost, and persistent cognitive manipulation. Therefore, we propose CogBias, a cognitive bias injection framework for LLMs. CogBias converts subjective preferences into optimization signals via a differentiable sentiment evaluator, uses a multi-objective loss to jointly constrain multiple dimensions, and constructs BitScout to locate critical bits, achieving targeted cognitive intervention under an ultra-sparse flip budget. Experiments on Llama-3.2-3B, Mist

c0199ffc8044e4f6c6b367b4.title_original: Instruction Self-Arbitration Is Not a Trust Boundary: Configuration-Dependent Tool Calls and External Enforcement in LLM Agents
c0199ffc8044e4f6c6b367b4.excerpt: arXiv:2608.28502v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM agents receive instructions from system prompts, users, memory and tools, and labels inside a shared context are not an enforceable trust boundary. The original keyword flag for detecting fabricated authority mostly matched negated phrases: two blind judges flagged the claim as fabricated in at most 1 of 150 GPT-4.1-mini responses. In a fully logged reflection re-run, responses that both express doubt and delete are rare after a reflection instruction (25 of 509 executions), and a casual request that gives a reason but claims no authority is executed by all ten endpoints. Source-format cues are linearly decodable (97.5-100% probe accuracy, four open-weight models), but a pre-specified crossed-probe test halted and gives no interpretable evidence of an abstract provenance representation, and steering did not move tool mention (0 of 1,895 trials, mention-scored). On the same 14,294 diverse-prompt trials across 29 endpoints, the rule fixed before collection gives an endpoint mean of 1.21%; a path-based reading chosen after the data were seen gives 12.9% [6.6-20.1%, 29 models]; any delete call gives 20.2%. In 1,350 sandbox trials, all 750 forged, tampered, replayed and unsigned records were rejected at admission and no

7cd2b0c16d4aa76492697a1a.title_original: 5GDescrambler: Locating, Descrambling, and Decoding 5G Scheduling Information (long version)
7cd2b0c16d4aa76492697a1a.excerpt: arXiv:2609.07367v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tracking users in 5G NR has recently been successfully demonstrated by exploiting various side-channels. This allows for identification of individuals, classification of user activity in real time as well as tracking by fingerprinting, affecting billions of users with a 5G subscription and companies with private 5G deployments. However, previous work relies on weak operator configurations that leak networking parameters--either the radio network temporary identifier (RNTI) or scrambling factor ($N_{ID}$) during handshake--or to inefficiently brute-force Downlink Control Information (DCI). In this paper we present a novel technique exploiting algebraic structure to reverse DCI scrambling, fully integrated into an open-source end-to-end binary DCI sniffing pipeline. It provides enabling input for subsequent attacks like live tracking of users and supports automatic detection of control channel configurations used. We demonstrate the robustness and performance of our approach with measurement campaigns against deployments of srsRAN, OpenAirInterface5G, and two commercial vendors. It reaches block error rates of less than $1\%$ at SNRs below expected values for efficient communication, while performing significantly faster on a reference sample than a previously suggested passive technique brute-forcing the required parameters. In addition, it is entirely passive and does not rely on any side-channel leakage.

5e96db98a559dc3577e8a458.title_original: SMS-delivered network-initiated SUPL on Pixel 8: a privacy assessment
5e96db98a559dc3577e8a458.excerpt: arXiv:2609.22900v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A SUPL\_INIT message is a network-initiated trigger that can be sent to a handset using an SMS to unilaterally start a location session: on receipt, the handset is instructed to determine its own position and report it, together with an identifier such as its IMSI, to a server specified in the message, without any action by the phone's user. The concern motivating this investigation is whether such a message could be used to silently exfiltrate a handset's location and subscriber identity to a server under an attacker's control. We investigated this on a Google Pixel 8 handset, which uses a Samsung Exynos modem and a Broadcom GPS/GNSS subsystem. We find no privacy issue: the handset never sends location data to an attacker-chosen server as a result of an unsolicited SUPL\_INIT delivered by SMS. We also examined an iPhone 8 (Qualcomm modem, iOS 16.7.11). On the handset studied SUPL is disabled, so it ignores any SUPL\_INIT and opens no SUPL connections of its own. More generally, iOS acts on a SUPL\_INIT only during an emergency call, and connects only to a server matching the carrier's configured one.

c749696e1bb337104a1e34dd.title_original: Protecting CPU AI On Edge TEEs: WebAssembly's Promise and Practical Challenges
c749696e1bb337104a1e34dd.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12050v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI models on edge hardware contain important intellectual property (IP), but an adversary can steal it when they achieve root access. Trusted Execution Environments (TEE) like Arm TrustZone protect against these Operating System (OS) level attacks. However, they are challenging to use. More precisely, it is difficult to run unaltered applications inside a TEE. This work presents a solution that allows the execution of unaltered AI models, compiled to WebAssembly, on the WebAssembly Micro Runtime (WAMR) in OP-TEE for Arm TrustZone. Additionally, this work provides an AI model distributor that encrypts the WebAssembly binary and places the encryption key in one of the device's fuses. This way, only the WAMR Trusted Application (TA) in OP-TEE can decrypt and execute the AI model. A thorough evaluation of our solution shows that it incurs an additional overhead of 22% in comparison to an application manually ported to OP-TEE, while also facilitating the execution of unaltered AI models with an additional inference latency of 6% without significant porting effort. Overall, there is a pressing need to safeguard the IP of AI models and this work shows that there is a real promise in WebAssembly, but there remain some practical challenges.

071d22e93209abfbe1f74053.title_original: DICE: Tilting the Odds through Interface Attacks on System One Model
071d22e93209abfbe1f74053.excerpt: arXiv:2610.14404v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: System One models offer typed judgments that applications can turn into decisions. Their answers, however, are conditional on the state and question supplied by surrounding components, and on how the application uses the response. We study this boundary in a Jev-based pipeline with bounded substitutions at three adapter outputs: state extraction, question generation, and output interpretation. Across three small synthetic studies, each adapter can change the final decision while Jev and its authentic API responses remain outside attacker control. The cases expose distinct failures of source fidelity, answer meaning, and response relevance. Checks that bind these relationships stopped the corresponding interventions we tested, although source verification also rejected some valid clean decisions. The pilot identifies where correct request-level judgments can lose their connection to the original task; it does not estimate the prevalence of these failures in deployed systems.

45c6277b125f640d35055e1f.title_original: A Quantum Approach For Reducing Communications in Classical Secure Computations with Long Outputs
45c6277b125f640d35055e1f.excerpt: arXiv:2310.05213v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How could quantum cryptography help us achieve what are not achievable in classical cryptography? In this work we study the classical cryptographic problem that two parties would like to perform secure computations with long outputs. As a basic primitive and example, we first consider the following problem which we call secure function sampling with long outputs: suppose $f:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow \{0,1\}^m$ is a public, efficient classical function, where $m$ is big; Alice would like to sample $x$ from its domain and sends $f(x)$ to Bob; what Bob knows should be no more than $f(x)$ even if it behaves maliciously. Classical cryptography, like FHE and succinct arguments [Gen09,Kil92,HW15], allows us to achieve this task within communication complexity $O(n+m)$; could we achieve this task with communication complexity independent of $m$? In this work, we first design a quantum cryptographic protocol that achieves secure function sampling with approximate security, within $O(n)$ communication (omitting the dependency on the security parameter and error tolerance). We also prove the classical impossibility using techniques in [HW15], which means that our protocol indeed achieves a type of quantum advantage. Building on the secure function sampling protocol, we further construct protocols for general secure two-party computations [Yao86,GB01] with approximate security, with communication complexity only depending on the input

58a351fa6864386abc62d060.title_original: Quantitative Quantum Soundness for Bipartite Compiled Bell Games via the Sequential NPA Hierarchy
58a351fa6864386abc62d060.excerpt: arXiv:2507.17006v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Compiling Bell games under cryptographic assumptions replaces the need for physical separation, allowing nonlocality to be probed with a single untrusted device. While Kalai et al. (STOC'23) showed that this compilation preserves quantum advantages, its quantitative quantum soundness has remained an open problem. We address this gap with two primary contributions. First, we establish the first quantitative quantum soundness bounds for all bipartite compiled Bell games via a newly formalized convergent sequential Navascu\'es-Pironio-Ac\'in (NPA) hierarchy: any polynomial-time prover's score is controlled by a finite-level hierarchy value, and finite-level convergence gives a negligible gap to the commuting quantum value, or to the tensor-product quantum value under flat optimality. Second, we develop the sequential NPA hierarchy as a computational tool of independent interest, establishing its convergence and a stopping criterion based on flatness, and identifying its conic dual as a sparse SOS hierarchy.

8d346ccbac9c8a54c8b71bbb.title_original: Multi-Criteria Routing for Cryptographic Key Exchange in QKD Networks: Survey, Taxonomy, and a Conceptual Optimization Framework
8d346ccbac9c8a54c8b71bbb.excerpt: arXiv:2511.15465v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) networks enable unconditionally secure key exchange using quantum mechanical principles. However, routing cryptographic keys across multi-hop quantum networks introduces challenges unique to quantum communication. This survey analyzes and classifies 26 routing strategies proposed between 2013 and 2024 for terrestrial, satellite, and hybrid QKD infrastructures. Dynamic, key-aware routing algorithms have been shown to reduce service rejection rates by 25-40% compared to static shortest-path methods by incorporating real-time key pool availability and link error rates. Multi-path strategies improve resilience against trusted-node compromise by distributing keys across disjoint routes, albeit with an increase in key consumption of 30-60%. SDN-based orchestration frameworks emerge as essential enablers of flexible, QoS-aware routing for hybrid networks integrating terrestrial fibers and intermittent satellite links. Critical research directions include reducing dependence on trusted nodes through quantum repeaters or post-quantum cryptography, developing standardized key management interfaces for interoperability, and adopting AI-driven predictive routing for adapting to fluctuating network states. This comprehensive synthesis of routing algorithms, performance trade-offs, and unresolved issues offers practical guidance for engineering secure, adaptable, and large-scale QKD networks capable of

f5eec26c3d210082897551bd.title_original: PTOPOFL: Topology-Guided Personalised Federated Learning with Persistent-Homology Client Descriptors
f5eec26c3d210082897551bd.excerpt: arXiv:2603.04323v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Clustered and personalised federated learning (FL) needs a signal telling the server which clients should share a model. Most methods derive it from losses or model updates that must be recomputed during training. We study pTopoFL, which derives it once, before training, from a compact persistent-homology (PH) descriptor of each client's feature distribution: the server clusters clients on these descriptors, weights them within clusters, and runs blended clustered local gradient descent, returning one personalised model per cluster. For strongly convex, smooth losses we analyse the complete procedure: for any partition, one round is a contraction with factor (1-eta*mu)^tau; the fixed point is characterised by a local-step drift bound, an exact formula for the effective strength of blending (which yields a calibration rule) and a stochastic floor exposing a bias-variance trade-off of clustering; and personalisation lowers the heterogeneity floor in proportion to a measurable share of the dispersion of client optima. Experiments on synthetic federations, a label-skew benchmark and a real four-hospital dataset confirm the theory and delimit the method. e3d0ae14c17bd4c059d375f9.title_original: Quantifying Memorization and Privacy Risks in Genomic Language Models
e3d0ae14c17bd4c059d375f9.excerpt: arXiv:2603.08913v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Genomic language models (GLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning representations of DNA sequences, enabling advances in variant prediction, regulatory element identification, and cross-task transfer learning. However, as these models are increasingly trained or fine-tuned on sensitive genomic cohorts, they risk memorizing specific sequences from their training data, raising serious concerns around privacy, data leakage, and regulatory compliance. Despite growing awareness of memorization risks in general-purpose language models, little systematic evaluation exists for these risks in the genomic domain, where data exhibit unique properties such as a fixed nucleotide alphabet, strong biological structure, and individual identifiability. We present a comprehensive, multi-vector privacy evaluation framework designed to quantify memorization risks in GLMs. Our approach integrates three complementary risk assessment methodologies: perplexity-based detection, canary sequence extraction, and membership inference. These are combined into a unified evaluation pipeline that produces a worst-case memorization risk score. To enable controlled evaluation, we plant canary sequences at varying repetition rates into both synthetic and real genomic datasets, allowing precise quantification of how repetition and training dynamics influence memorization. We evaluate our framework across multiple GLM architectures, examining the

8b323a4a582eb03ff14f4f3d.title_original: Cyclic Equalizability Characterized by Parikh Vectors
8b323a4a582eb03ff14f4f3d.excerpt: arXiv:2604.19504v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cyclic equalizability is a notion introduced by Shinagawa and Nuida in 2025, in the study of card-based cryptography. Informally, a collection of words is cyclically equalizable if, by inserting the same letters at the same positions in all words, they can be transformed into words that are cyclic shifts of one another. Shinagawa and Nuida showed that two binary words of equal length are cyclically equalizable if and only if they have the same Hamming weight. They also posed the problem of characterizing cyclic equalizability over larger alphabets. In this paper, we completely characterize cyclic equalizability for two words over an arbitrary finite alphabet by proving that two words are cyclically equalizable if and only if they have the same Parikh vector.

c24f3e196ad55fd49a331f0f.title_original: How To Track Qubits Through Space and Time (Or: Sailing in a Quantum Boat)
c24f3e196ad55fd49a331f0f.excerpt: arXiv:2605.30732v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While quantum position verification aims to certify a prover's location using quantum information, existing security definitions only guarantee that part of the successful adversarial party is in the claimed location. This leaves open the possibility that a distributed team of adversaries can jointly simulate a prover in a way that defeats the intended meaning of `being at a location' in position-based cryptography. We introduce stronger notions of position verification that we call quantum localization, which requires that there is a specified, unclonable state at the verified spacetime point-and that this state can be found nowhere else. We show that quantum localization leads naturally to a meaningful notion of trajectory verification, in which quantum information is verifiably tracked through space and time. We construct quantum localization and trajectory verification protocols using quantum anchor states, which generalize coset states from unclonable cryptography. The security of our schemes is proven in the classical oracle (i.e. ideal obfuscation) model, which can be heuristically instantiated in the plain model using post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation. We also introduce and instantiate the concept of functionality localization, which guarantees that the adversary has the ability to compute a secret function at the verified spacetime point, and this function cannot be computed anywhere else. adb8ae043aba93edd0cc5f80.title_original: CHERI-D: Secure and efficient inline object ID for CHERI temporal memory safety
adb8ae043aba93edd0cc5f80.excerpt: arXiv:2606.19055v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose CHERI-D, an architectural extension to CHERI that supports efficient temporal memory safety. Efficient memory safety is an increasing priority for programming languages, operating systems, and hardware designs, and CHERI is a leading hardware/software system that provides native spatial safety and a foundation for temporal memory safety. Due to CHERI lacking intrinsic architectural support for temporal memory safety, the state-of-the-art CHERI temporal safety solution, Cornucopia Reloaded, is a software-based solution that provides use-after-reallocation (UAR) protections instead of the stronger use-after-free (UAF) mitigation, and suffers performance overhead due to delayed reallocation and revocation. CHERI-D associates object identification (ID) metadata with capability pointers to provide temporal integrity of allocations. CHERI spatial safety allows CHERI-D to store object IDs safely inline with allocation data, potentially within unused fragmentation. Evaluated in simulation and in hardware, CHERI-D significantly reduces the revocation overhead of Cornucopia Reloaded while allowing it to support strict use-after-free mitigation.

3d998853a7ee424df5a170bb.title_original: A Trust Ledger and an Execution Check for CPG-Based C-to-Lean 4 Autoformalization: Separating Declined from Silently Incorrect Translations
3d998853a7ee424df5a170bb.excerpt: arXiv:2609.38237v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Verifying large C codebases requires translating them into formally checkable semantics, but most autoformalization work reports a single aggregate success rate that conflates two different failure modes: code the translator declined to handle and code the translator translated incorrectly. Applied to a re-export of the SQLite source tree (8{,}602 functions, over 1.5~million AST nodes), the exporter translates 5{,}222 functions (60.7\%) hole-free, of which only 2{,}134 (24.8\%) are call-closed, a $2.4\times$ gap a single rate would hide. aaba9e6b332c2478eefd28de.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13357v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings pass through multiple networks and systems before automated interpretation, making patient metadata vulnerable to loss.
